CHINESE STEAMSHIP CREWS On the Orders of the Day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Immigration and Colonization):
speechtext:
On Thursday April
24, the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) stated:
According to the Halifax Herald of April 14, forty-nine orientals have arrived there to work on the Nova Scotia coal boats. Subsequent investigation seems to show that the Chinese landed from the s.s. Cedric, Pier 2, Halifax, direct from Liverpool, England, having arrived there from Canton via the Suez canal, and that these Chinese are imported from the Orient as crews for the Wabana, Daghild, and other vessels of Canadian registration. These Chinese are acting in the capacity of sailors, quartermaster, oilers, stockers, stewards and cooks; they are to relieve the hardy Nova Scotians. The Herald states that they are in bond and that permission to land and place the Chinamen on the various allotted vessels was given under letter received from the Deputy Minister of Immigration at Ottawa.
I promised the hon. member to inquire and advise him, and I have this information:
On the 3rd instant a telegram was received by the Department of Immigration and Colonization from Mr. J. R. Mclsaac of the Steel Corporation, stating that, owing to difficulty in getting Canadian crews to remain with their steamers after signing up, it was proposed to bring Chinese from England, a number to sail on the Cedric on the 5th instant, and the remainder, about nine, to come forward by a later boat to complete a crew now on this side.
The corporation gave the assurance that, except in the case of one vessel, the Chinese were to be confined to employment as firemen and cooks and that it was hoped to secure white men for the other classes of work on
Point oj Order-Mr. Boys

their steamers. The department consented to the request of the British Empire Steel Corporation on the understanding that arrangements were completed for guarding the Chinese and that the corporation would be responsible for all penalties under the Chinese Immigration Act until a bond, satisfactory to the department, was furnished.
A bond for $105,000 has been deposited with the department, this bond to cover 105 Chinese who are to be engaged on the steamships Rosecastle, Daghild, Wabana, Lingan, Hochelaga and Kamouraska, plying between the ports of Sydney, Louisburg, Halifax, St. John and Montreal. While the bond is for $105,000 it provides for a penalty of $1,000 in the case of each chinaman engaged on the steamships mentioned. Only 76 Chinamen have come forward or are coming forward under this arrangement with the Steel corporation, the bond covering also the cases of 29 Chinese who came forward last fall for employment on the Kamouraska. There are precedents in the department for action of this nature.
These Chinese are regarded as non-immigrants and the bond deposited by the British Empire Steel Corporation will be retained until the department is satisfied that all of the Chinese covered by the same have been checked out of Canada.
I should like to ask just in this connection whether this arrangement by which Chinese are allowed here under bond is not worse than any form of peonage.

speechtext: The House resumed from Friday, April 25th, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Acting Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Woodsworth.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext: Before the debate proceeds, I might ask hon. members if they have any further remarks to offer concerning the point of order which was raised the other day. My ruling is, of course, ready to be delivered, but I should not like to prevent any hon. member from stating his point of view.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, after your announcement, I realise the futility of taking up much time in discussing this matter, but we deem it of suffi-

cient importance at all events to place ourselves very definitely on record in connection with it. I do not propose to quote again the amendment that was moved before recess last Friday, nor the amendment which was moved after recess, at eight o'clock. They will both be found in the remarks of my leader (Mr. Meighen) which appear in Hansard of last Friday. I do, however, want to support the contention that he then made, and I think as a preliminary to what I have to say, I should read the rule of our own .House upon the question. Rule No. 77 reads:
If any motion be made in the House for any public aid or charge upon the people-
"Charge upon the people" are the words that I wish to emphasize.
-the consideration and debate thereof may not be presently entered upon, but shall be adjourned to such further day as the House thinks fit to appoint; and then it shall be referred to a committee of the whole House, before any resolution or vote of the House do pass thereupon.
This rule has obtained in our parliament for half a century. As far as I have been able to read, it has obtained in the British House for 200 years, and I submit that it should not be lightly disregarded. The objection is two-fold. In the first place, it is contended that the amendment that was made by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth), that reached this House at six o'clock and that was seconded by the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw) was subsequently altered. The first point I wish to make is this, that the only amendment before this House that had a seconder was the amendment moved by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg and placed in the hands of the Speaker before recess. After recess-and we are led to believe as the result of some discussion owing- to the fact that that amendment was considered not to be in order-it was changed. Let us first see what is the duty of the Chair on receiving a motion which is considered unparliamentary. Rule 46 reads:
Whenever the Speaker is of opinion that a motion offered to the House is contrary to the rules and privileges of parliament, he shall apprise the House thereof immediately, before putting the question thereon and quote the rule or authority applicable to the case.
There is no question that the amendment which was moved in the House by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg (Mr. Woodsworth) was presented to the Chair. There can be little or no question that that amendment was out of order; and I submit Sir, that the first thing to have been done in the circumstances was to have had recourse tc

Point of Order-Mr. Boys
rule 46. That was not done; but for reasons which cannot be fully disclosed, the amendment that was put by the Chair after recess was absolutely different in form from the original motion. It was different in parar graphs A., B. and C. of the operative part, inasmuch as it involved entirely new features; I refer now to those provisions of the amended motion relating to all natural resources. Now, what authority was there to make that change? Who seconded that amendment? I submit, Sir, that it had no seconder then, nor has it any seconder at the present time. I do not even know that the hon. member for West Calgary (Mr. Shaw), who did second the amendment as originally moved by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg, was present when the substituted motion was put to the House. I therefore contend that inasmuch as the second amendment as put by the Chair had no seconder it is consequently not properly before the House at the present moment; and I submit that there is no power whatever to make any such changes in the original motion as were made. It would seem to me that if there is any distinction between what has been done in the matter in hand and what might be done in connection with a formal notice of motion, which would first have to appear in Votes and Proceedings, there should be more formality and greater stricture in the case of such a motion as was submitted to the House by the hon. member for Centre Winnipeg. Let me quote May at page 216:
A modification of a notice of motion standing upon the notice paper is permitted, if the amended notice does not exceed the scope of the original notice. If a motion is proposed, which differs materially from the terms of the notice, it can only be made with the consent of the House, or upon a renewal of the notice.
I would direct the attention of the House again to the ground upon which any modification of a notice of motion may be made, that is to say,-
If the amended notice does not exceed the scope of the original notice.
Now, Sir, there is no doubt that the substituted amendment does differ absolutely from the motion as originally presented to the House. And if in connection with a formal notice of motion which appears in Votes and Proceedings no change may be made without the consent of the House, how much more imperative, may we argue, that in relation to a matter of this kind, whereof there is not even intimation beforehand, there shall be no change unless the House is apprised of the fact. The amendment has been changed; no one contends for a moment that it has not. I do not know
what authority may be cited in support of that change. I am aware of course that there is a reference to a similar situation in the American rules of procedure, but I submit that such would not be a proper authority for this House. Indeed, I do not even know whether the rules observed in the United States are identical with ours. In any event I contend that no precedent available to this parliament can be found for the change that has been made in the present instance; there is no precedent so far as either the British practice or our own is concerned.
Let me now come to the second point. I have already shown what has been the practice in this House for half a century and in the British parliament for two centuries; and I find in Bourinot at page 430 the following :
It is now a fixed principle of constitutional government that all propositions for the imposition of taxes should emanate from the ministry.
At page 431 Bourinot says:
All the authorities go to show that, when the government have formally submitted to the House the question for the revision of customs and excise duties, it is competent for a member "to propose in committee to substitute another tax of equivalent amount for that proposed by ministers, the necessity of new taxation to a given extent being declared on behalf of the Crown". It is also competent for any member to propose another scheme of taxation for the same purpose, as a substitute for the government plan. But it is not regular to propose a new and distinct tax, which is not a mere increase or diminution of a duty upon an article already recommended by government for taxation, though it is the function of this committee to impose rather than to repeal taxes.
I submit that there is nothing whatever in that proposition which brings the present case within the category of exceptions. In the first place, there is no tax at all proposed at the present time and therefore there is no question of substituting any equivalent of a plan proposed by the government. An abundance of authority may be cited in support of the position I take on this matter for, as I have said, there are precedents covering a period of some two hundred years. Let me now refer to Redlich's The Procedure of the House of Commons, Vol. Ill at page 121. Referring to this very principle which has been dealt with in May, he says:
It is one of the oldest of the standing orders now in force: first enunciated on the 11th of July 1713, it has twice been expressly reaffirmed, on the 25th of June 1852 and on the 20th of March 1866. It runs as follows: This House will receive-
And I may remark that this is order 66 of the British House-
This House will receive no petition for any sum relating to public service, or proceed upon any motion
Point of Order-Mr. Speaker

for a grant or charge upon the public revenue, whether payable out of the consolidated fund or out of money to be provided by parliament, unless recommended from the Crown.
I think it wise to read a few lines further in order that we may gather some idea of the reasons which have prompted the continuance of this rule during the lengthy period I 'have mentioned.
By laying down this rule the House of Commons placed in the hands of the government all power of initiative in respect of the expenditure of public money, voluntarily resigning, both for itself as a body and for all its individual members, a privilege which in theory nobody had dreamed of contesting. Since the order was made it has not been competent for one or more unofficial members of the House to propose by motion or petition a grant of money for any purpose,-
Of course, there is authority to show that a charge is dealt with in exactly the same manner as a grant of money. That will be found in May.
-or for the House to act upon such a proposal unless the grant is asked for by the Crown: Only when this is done does the House vote definite sums for definite purposes.. ..The limitation of power effected by this action was undoubtedly a constitutional innovation of the deepest importance: It was, however, effected not, as might have been expected, by statute, but by a simple order of the House of Commons, liable at any moment to be repealed by an equally simple action: And yet for almost two hundred years it has been allowed to remain untouched as one of the main principles of
British finance.... The limitation is dictated by a
wise recognition of a serious danger: It is a measure of protection against the easy extravagance of a large assembly-
I am sure we all agree that this applies here now.
The House well knows how real the risk would be were each member entitled to use his eloquence and tactical ability for the purpose of calling the public credit of the country and its taxpaying capacity to the aid of any object in which he was interested.
We may have in mind, for example, Belle River at the present time.
State expenditure ought to be the expenditure of the responsible administration.
I submit, for the reasons given that the point of order raised by my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) is well taken; and I urge that the House should be cautious in permitting any innovation in relation to so valuable and important a rule and one of such long standing.

On Thursday, April 24,
Mr. Woodsworth (Centre Winnipeg) closed his speech on the motion for the committee of Ways and Means by moving an amendment which was handed to me in order that I might put the question. It struck me as objectionable both in its form and subject matter. I always had some misgivings about the regularity of a similar amendment moved 
last year by Mr. Forke (Brandon), which, I think, might have served its purpose equally well had it been made less specific; for such motions, in order to be entertained, must be framed in abstract and general terms. Using my unquestioned authority in such a case. I conferred with the mover who agreed to make the necessary corrections.
This circumstance was admitted by Mr. Woodsworth on the floor of the House last Friday when he said:
In consultation with the Speaker and the authorities of the House-
Meaning the officers.
-I consented to make such changes in the resolution as seemed to be necessary or advisable in order that it should conform more nearly with the accepted usages of the House.
May, at page 247, says:
Even when notice of motion is not required-
As in the present case.
-the motion should be placed, in print or writing, in the Speaker's hands; as, except in the event of any informality in the form of the motion which may necessitate the Speaker's intervention, or may compel him to decline to put the question from the chair, the Speaker puts the question in the words of the mover.
An eminent authority, I may say, Redlich, Vol. 2, page 221, declares:
The possibility of the Speaker's refusing to allow a motion to be voted upon can only arise in the case of motions which are out of order either in their subject-matter or in their form. Such are motions which contain unbecoming expressions, infringe the rules of the House or contain reflections upon a vote of the House. Irregularities of this kind, may, under the Speaker's authority, be corrected by the clerks at the table.
Cushing, No. 1,233, says:
When a motion has been made merely, but not yet proposed or stated by the Speaker-
WTiich was the case in the present instance.
-the mover may withdraw, or modify it at his pleasure. This, consequently, is the time at which objections to motions, especially in point of form, are usually made, either by the Speaker, or by other members; upon which the mover may either explain and insist upon his motion, as it stands, or he may withdraw it altogether; or, adopting the suggestions for amendment, may modify it at his pleasure; and this power of the mover may be exercised, as it seems, without reference to his seconder, if the motion has been seconded.
I could either have ruled the amendment out of order or accepted the corrected draft. I deemed it advisable to follow the latter course, and in doing so I actually observed the customs and usages of this House. Had the question been put, I should certainly not have allowed it to be altered, because once the Speaker has stood up and read a motion

Point of Order-Mr. Speaker
or amendment, it ceases to be under the mover's control and can only be withdrawn by leave of the House to be granted without any negative voice, under rule 43, as so aptly remarked by the hon. member for Bonaven-ture (Mr. Marcil) speaking on the point of order.
As to the second objection raised by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Meighen) namely, that such a motion can only be made by a minister with the recommendation of the Crown, the theory is the same whether the motion relates to imposition of taxes or expenditure of public money, but it differs as to reduction of taxation. The amendment asks both for a reduction of certain customs duties and the taxation of unimproved land values. The decision given by Mr. Speaker Denison in 1858 settles the question as to levying new imposts or voting money which is governed by exactly the same principles. This most eminent authority said that there were indeed precedents in which the House had given an expression of its opinion that a certain vote of public money should be made; but it remained for the House to decide how far such intimations of opinion should bind it in the future course which it might adopt. Such intimations certainly created no new charge on the public, but they led to no practical result, and the whole question had to be begun again de novo, and to pass through all the forms of the House. (British Debates, 3rd Series, Yol. 151.
p. 1,168).
I may cite the following British precedents of motions made by private members for the expenditure of public money:
On the 9th July, 1858, the House carried an amendment expressing the opinion that the cost of the purification of the river Thames should be borne by the consolidated fund and the metropolitan ratepayers in equal proportion (Commons Journals, p. 113).
On the 24th April, 1863, it carried an amendment stating that the government should give sailors' homes such pecuniary assistance as in its judgment and discretion may be advisable (Commons Journals, p. 118).
On the 30th June, 1869, it adopted a motion stating it was expedient that the judges upon whom new duties and responsibilities might be imposed should receive additional remuneration of 300 pounds a year. (Commons Journals, p. 124.)
On March 13th, 1890, it carried an amendment that it was expedient that all deficiencies of the equipment of volunteers which were necessary to efficiency, and all debts of corps properly incurred on account of the same, be 98
made good from the public revenues. (Commons Journals, p. 145.)
There are, as we know, several Canadian precedents.
My immediate predecessor, Mr. Speaker Rhodes, said from the chair, on March 16, 1921,-and I agree with him-:
Taking the general view, it does seem to me that if the House were unduly to restrict hon. members in moving motions of this character it would serve to circumscribe debate to a very marked degree, because after all few resolutions are moved which would not in themselves, if carried into effect, involve the expenditure of public money. It seems to me the better principle would be to widen the rule as much as possible in order that the sense of the House may be taken upon these matters, it being understood in all cases that these resolutions merely involve an expression of opinion on the part of the House and that they do not affect the constitutional method of placing upon the government the responsibility of initiating all legislation which has for its object the expenditure of money.
The private member's right to move for a reduction of taxation suffers no limitation under our parliamentary rules and usages. May, at page 469, says:
It follows as a matter of course that a motion to alleviate the burthens upon the people is not within the scope of the standing orders relating to the imposition of charges upon the people. A bill for diminishing or repealing a tax or other public burthen, unless the imposition of a new tax is proposed by way of substitution, is introduced without the royal recommendation or preliminary committee stage. Amendments, also, strictly confined to relief from pecuniary burthens, can be considered both in committee and with the Speaker in the chair.
And at page 506 he says:
Proposals to reduce a burthen upon the people may be made in the House or in committee, no special form of procedure being prescribed for such a motion or for the introduction of bills which are strictly confined to the reduction of a tax or charge upon the people.
On the 18th May, 1920, Mr. Fielding-one of the oldest members of the House and, I must say, a very eminent authority on parliamentary procedure-moved an amendment on the motion for the committee of Ways and Means, specifically asking for a reduction of the customs duties on the instruments of production in the industries based on the natural resources of the Dominion.
On the ninth of June, 1919, Mr. McMaster moved, inter alia, in amendment to Sir Thomas White's budget proposals:
That the tariff should be so framed as to free the food of the people and the machinery used in the development of the natural resources of Canada, together with the raw material entering into the manufacture thereof.
It is true that rule 46 was overlooked in this case, but nobody suffered any prejudice or injustice from the fact. Whether or not the

House was apprised of any irregularity in the motion would not have divested Mr. Woodsworth of his right to modify it before it was put from the Chair. French constituents of the county of Gloucester may serve only to strengthen our adherence to and our love for British institutions.
Much has been said since the opening of the session in connection with the by-elections in the provinces by the sea. One of those elections at least has been the cause of a great column of smoke. The hon.

I believe that the hon. member for Kent . (Mr. Doucet) is treading on unsafe ground, first, in trying to defend his party from the just retribution which is its due, and second, in committing for all time to come the peaceful peasants of the good old county of Kent to a policy of protection. The Budget-Mr. Robicliaud
Much has been said throughout the press and otherwise about the so-called Maritime rights. If such rights exist, and I believe they do exist but only in the abstract, it would be interesting to note who have been responsible for whatever is wrong. Hon. gentlemen representing New Brunswick constituencies who sit to your immediate left, Mr. Speaker, have, at meetings in the constituency of Kent and in the city of Halifax, taken the ground that the present government should be saddled with the responsibility for whatever may be wrong with the present status of the Maritime provinces. But my contention is that those provinces are now suffering from the evils inflicted on them during the ten years of maladminstration which preceded the election of 1921. By the terms of confederation we were given a railroad which was to unite us more closely with the Upper and Lower Canadas of that day; the object was to repay us for the concessions we had to make in the interest of our sister provinces in the West. But what happened? In 1915 legislation was passed with the intention of taking over branch lines, and especially in the Maritime provinces. The purpose of the legislation was good but in giving effect to it the policy was overdone. Certain interests that had made large investments in railways and practically lost those investments manifested a desire to -feed at the public crib. In 1917 a policy of nationalization of railways was embarked upon by the federal administration of the time, and the Maritime provinces saw the Intercolonial, a road which was built to give effect to the confederation pact, taken from them and merged into the great National system. _ That action constitutes part of our grievances in the Maritime provinces. I submit that the Intercolonial railway-which as I already said formed part of the inalienable property of the Maritime provinces-which was built to promote the best interests of that part of Canada, should have been left intact to carry out the object for which it was constructed. An analysis of the stand which hon. gentlemen opposite from New Brunswick have taken indicates that they have been actuated by partisan and not disinterested motives. We know where the trouble lies for the present condition of affairs and where the remedy can be found. Much has been said with respect to the rights of the Maritime provinces, but I doubt whether any one party holds the brief to defend those rights. My hon. friend (Mr. Baxter) and the hon. member for Kent have thrown upon 98i
the present government the blame for the grievances which exist to-day and have practically made the issue a political one. Now, to show what serious minded men in the Maritime provinces are thinking about in regard to those provinces and their rights, and the direction in which they think a remedy can be found, I am going to quote what the Hon. C. W. Robinson, a man of great experience and clear vision, who is now Minister of Lands and Mines in New Brunswick, stated in a communication which was published by the St. John Telegraph in January last. I want to read the statement just to show that the question of rights of the Maritime provinces should not be considered a political football, but rather that it should be treated in a serious light by the men of all parties and regarded as too sacred to be dealt with in a political way. This is what Mr. Robinson said:
Our influence is naturally declining along with our proportion of population. In 1867 we had, roughly, one-Quarter the population of Canada while to-day we have only one-eighth. And the outlook of the future does not indicate any improvement. Under the B.N.A. Act, unfortunately, as provinces are not treated alike. British Columbia, for instance, was safeguarded against a reduction in representation, while we have no such protection, and our representation is diminishing. With such a situation staring us in the face, our people are not happy. We are peculiarly sensitive to any action on the part of the Dominion which seems to encroach on what we consider our ancient rights and privileges. The flamboyant prophecies of the Fathers of Confederation as to the future development of our harbours have not materialized. These harbours are convenient national terminals in time of war, but Portland, Maine, looms large in times of peace. When car shortage becomes acute, it is the Maritimes which suffer most. The cost of transportation hems us in- this is not an unmixed evil-it is driving large business houses to establish centres of business in the Maritimes, on the one hand while on the other it cruelly handicaps those local industries which desire to extend their trade to the west. Perhaps we should turn our eyes oceanward and seek to reap some of the advantages of the Maritime position.
Some of us thought that freer trade with the States would help out the situation, but the verdict of the people closed that door most effectively.
Mr. Robinson, goes on to say:
Recently some progress has been made in improving our condition. The establishment of the Atlantic region of the C.N.R., with headquarters at Moncton, was a long step in advance.
The encouragement of our winter ports and giving them a preference under the Fielding tariff is already having its effect. The car shortage seems to have been remedied. The efforts now being made by the C.N.R. to develop greater tourist travel in our direction is bound to have a beneficial result. It is in the power of the railway to do much along this and other lines which will contribute to greater progress and prosperity for this part of the country, and I have confidence that the future will show that they are fully seized of their responsibilities, and in their own interest will assist greatly in our development.

The Budget-Mr. Robichaud
We must realize that national conditions demand that some economics be made. While it is necessaiy and quite proper for us to keep before the rest of Canada the matters which are so vital to our people, we must also think in wider circles, take pride in our country as a whole, get busy, forget our troubles, take advantage of our many opportunities, and go forth to fill our place in the larger prosperity which, I believe, is slowly but surely coming our way.
This, Mr. Speaker, is to show this House and the country what little, if any, shade of political partisanship our public men of New Brunswick are introducing into this question of Maritime rights. The Hon. Fred. Magee, the minister without portfolio in the New Brunswick legislature, a man standing high in the esteem of the people of the Maritime provinces, a man who has made a special study of Maritime rights, and whose opinion is regarded as commensurate with his immense business ability, gave the following opinion in an article he published in the St. John Telegraph Journal on the 19th January last. Referring to Maritime rights and political partisanship, the hon. gentleman, in referring to a serious question which had been put to him by the editor of the Journal, said:
In reply to your question number two as to what is the best way to secure our " rights," so called, permit me to say that we must have abolition of the doctrine of Maritime rights as a party dogma. It is a Maritime, not a party matter. No party includes all the Maritime patriots and no party should so imagine. Let this be understood. Our federal representatives should co-operate, as party allegiance is not a means to an end, in this case. Careful, sensible, practical, straightforward, impersonal, unemotional and non-partisan presentation of our case at opportune times by those we send to Ottawa is essential. Federal members please note.
In conclusion I still maintain that legislative union with Nova Scotia should be consummated that we may wield greater power and influence in the National council of Canada in which Maritime statesmen have always played a prominent and important part. I
I may interject right here, Mr. Speaker, that the Hon. Mr. Magee, is a fervent believer in Maritime union. I doubt very much if he is right in his belief, but after all it is very pleasant to know that he has, in the representatives from Nova Scotia on the floor of this House, quite a number of supporters in this regard.
It has been stated that this government had neglected to take care, or had refrained from taking care, of the rights of the Maritime provinces. It has also been stated that this government was going too far in its policy or in its endeavour to maintain public works in the Maritime provinces. It has been further stated that the matter of public works was becoming a public scandal. These public works have even been termed the notorious pork barrel. I wish to take exception Mr. Speaker,

to these insinuations. It matters not whether they come from Grattan O'Leary, or whether they have been inserted in MacLean's Magazine, the Montreal Star, or the Moncton Times, I claim these insinuations reflect upon the honesty of my constituents as well as upon the honesty of the representatives of the country. In support of my assertion, Mr. Speaker, I may say that when the late administration went out of power on the 4th August, 1911 the fishermen of the county of Gloucester enjoyed a large amount of protection in the way of public accommodation. A good start had been made in the improvement of our harbours, and industry itself was in a very flourishing condition. Much has been said about what has been recently termed, as I said before, the pork barrel. MacLean's Magazine was especially to the fore in articles relating to the doings of this government is looking to the upkeep of those public works in the Maritime provinces. My constituents in the county of Gloucester regard these insinuations as a reflection upon their integrity and loyalty as citizens of Canada. If we want to reconstruct or put our public works on a sound footing, it is because our people desire to pursue their occupations and to remain in the country. It is because we, in the county of Gloucester prize more than anything else the old homestead, and those parcels of the historic land of Evangeline, which were allotted to the sturdy fishermen of the Maritime provinces.
To demonstrate our position before the House and the country, let me enumerate different public works which had been neglected under the late administration, and point out to you the condition in which we found them when the late government went out of power. Of course these details are not very pleasant to listen to, but I want to make clear my point on this subject, and to show that we are not indulging in the county of Gloucester in the luxury of the so-called pork barrel. I want to make it plain that if we want our share of the public money, it is because of our industrial needs, because our fishermen, through their patriotism, desire to remain in the country, because they wish to eke out a fair living for their families, and because they are engaged in an industry which must be maintained for the benefit of Canada.
In enumerating the different public works which have been neglected by the late administration in Gloucester county, I may mention first the Miscou wharf built on the north shore of Miscou harbour where the Baie des Chaleurs herring industry is carried

on most extensively. Situated on the island of Miscou, this wharf was built some 20 years ago and it was of the greatest service to the one thousand inhabitants on that island. In 1921 we found that the superstructure of that wharf was almost completely gone and crumbling into pieces. I would ask any hon. member if he thinks it would be an extravagant expenditure to keep up and repair that wharf for the benefit of those poor people. Some $10,000 will have to be spent by this government: $1,000 two years ago, $3,000 last year, and the House will be asked to vote a further sum of $5,500 this year in order to complete the repairs upon the Miscou wharf. If we have to spend $10,000 to repair a structure which cost the government some $30,000 to build, is it not undeniable evidence, that public works were shamefully neglected by the late administration?
We have another wharf some few miles away at Petite Lameque, where a large fleet of fishing vessels are engaged in the fishing industry. It was found, when the late administration went out of power, that the flooring of that wharf was practically all gone and that it had to be rebuilt immediately. In that instance, we had to spend two years ago a further sum of $2,000 out of the public treasury. At Lameque where we have one of the most important groups of fishermen in the Maritime provinces and where at the expense of some SS0.000 of public money a public wharf had been built under the Laurier administration, it was found, as I say, that the structure was broken up, the flooring was gone and the stringers were breaking through,
I may state also that the caretaker of that wharf during the late administration wrote to the Department of Public Works telling them that the wharf was in a dangerous condition and, as a reply, he received orders to close the wharf if it was dangerous for public use. That is the kind of regard that the late administration had for our fishermen in the county of Gloucester.
At Shippigan, we found a wharf altogether too small for the great bulk of business that was being carried on there. The wharf was congested from one end to the other. Repeated demands had been made upon the late administration to have the evil remedied, but as in other cases in the constituency of Gloucester, the late administration turned a deaf ear to our legitimate demands. The result was that this government at the last session of parliament caused to be voted a further sum of $7,000 to enlarge and repair the wharf at Shippigan. Under the judicious supervision of the present Department of
Public Works, there has been created at Shippigan, at a very trifling expense, one of the finest fishing docks in the Maritime provinces, a dock that can shelter the whole of Gloucester county's magnificent fishing fleet, a dock which is absolutely necessary for the benefit of the people there, and a dock which is certainly a credit to the present government.
At Caraquet-and I am sorry the hon. member for St. John city and counties of St. John and Albert (Mr. Baxter) is not in his seat when I make mention of this structure-we found a great fishing fleet without a wharf on which to land their fish. We found that the old government wharf had crumbled; that all but two or three of the spans were broken. The fishermen were left without a wharf, and it was up to this administration to come to their aid and spend at Caraquet a further sum of about $30,000 in order to enable them to pursue their occupation. The hon. member for St. John city, in his visit to Caraquet last year, while trying to reinvigorate the fragmentary remnants of the Tory party in my constituency, paid a visit to that wharf, and he admitted that the poor fishermen of Caraquet were in a very undesirable plight. The result of my effort in this regard is that a sum of $27,500 has been placed in the main estimates of this year for the reconstruction of that wharf, and I sincerely hope that when this money is voted, neither the hon. member for St. John city nor any other representing Ms party in New Brunswick, nor Grattan O'Leary, nor the Montreal Star, nor MacLean's magazine will throw in the face of the people of Gloucester county that this wharf has been built for the purpose of capturing the votes of my constituents.
I am about half through with wharves in the county of Gloucester. The fishing industry of my constituency amounts to over $3,250,000 a year. We have engaged in tb<"-industry a large fleet of fishing boats owned by men who with their predecessors have followed that industry for over a century, and I maintain that is is the duty of this government to keep that industry in such a shape as to encourage those who are engaged in it to continue to pursue their occupation and to remain within the bounds of this country.
At Inkerman, when I was given the honour to represent my constituency, I found the farmers and fishermen were forced to use sleds drawn by horses to land the fruits of their labour, the products of the sea. I found that those who were not equipped with a horse and sled had to land their fish over the railing of the Mghway bridge. I made cer-

tain representations to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. King, Kootenay) upon the strength of which there was built at Inkerman a wharf that greatly accommodates that very progressive little village. This wharf was made available to my constituents at Inker-man at the nominal cost of $3,500. At Grande Anse we find that a dock which was built by the Laurier government prior to the elections of 1911 had been left absolutely without repairs throughout the whole administration of the late government, not a dollar having been spent upon it. The basin has been allowed to become silted in those places where vessels of any considerable size should be able to come in, so that where formerly there was a depth of from ten to fifteen feet of water we find to-day that our poor fishermen are obliged to use rowboats instead of fishing schooners, for there is no more than from two or three feet of water.
Now, in spite of the large expenditures to which this government is subjected, I am bound to say that the necessity for further expenditure at Grande Anse is becoming increasingly keener. We have there a class of fishermen who are second to none in the Maritime provinces; but they have had to abandon their occupation and are now leaving our country and going to the United States. This is due to no fault whatever of the present government but to the neglect of the late administration; for the country cannot afford to spend a further amount of between $30,000 and $35,000 in order to alleviate the difficulties that are being felt in that vicinity at the present time but I hope that the time is not far distant when this work will be undertaken and carried to completion. At Stonehaven, I heard a few days ago, the structure of the wharf has gone and, that it must be rebuilt, and rebuilt without further delay. At Petit Roeher, at the time the late administration went out of power, the breakwater, owing to the action of the sea, was breaking in, and had to be repaired by the present government at a cost of some $14,000.
An important matter that interests my constituents is the protection which is necessary for the fishermen at Shippigan gully, which is the eastern entrance of Shippigan harbour. Shippigan gully is the only shelter between the Gaspe coast and IMiramichi bay, for the eighteen hundred fishermen of Gloucester county who are engaged in the fishing industry; there is no other place where our fishermen can put in in case of a storm. This passage has been so badly neglected that in 1913 some fourteen fishermen lost their lives off the island of Miscou. This unfortunate fatality was inevitable inasmuch as the fisher-

men could not depend upon Shippigan gully as an entrance in the darkness of night. I brought this matter to the attention of the present Minister of Public Works and also to the attention of the Department of Marine and Fisheries with the result that the lighting and buoy system in Shippigan gully has been so improved that it is one of the best that we have in eastern New Brunswick. I have enumerated the improvements that have been made, as well as the difficulties which our fishermen have laboured under in the past, in order to show to the country that after all this so-called pork barrel is not a vote-catcher but is an absolute necessity for the pioneer settlers in the Maritime provinces.
Before I resume my seat I desire to deal for a few moments with the budget, and I trust that hon. members will not tax me with exceeding my privileges. The study given to the budget by hon. members who have already spoken is commanding the keenest interest of the public, and from what I have been able to gather it would seem that hope and courage, perseverance and endurance will be restored in this land which we have learned so deeply to love and cherish. Apart from the pessimistic views expressed by hon. members to your immediate left, Mr. Speaker, there is a general manifestation of contentment and satisfaction in the tone of our deliberations; and this manifestation, displayed as it is by the majority of the representatives of the people, is an undeniable evidence of the feeling which is being credited throughout the country by the efforts of this government to extricate it from the predicament in which it was placed by the late administration It has been abundantly demonstrated that the tariff reforms brought down by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) are quite acceptable to the people of the country and that they are perhaps the best that could have been submitted for our consideration. An analysis of the budget by an unbiased mind will readily show that a great measure of relief is afforded the common people of Canada, who have suffered more than any other class during the period of deflation which has so seriously undermined their position in this country. A substantial reduction in taxation will be enjoyed by the poorer classes, and a large measure of confidence will be created throughout the country, confidence which will have an immediate effect upon the exodus of our people and which will stimulate business and hasten a much needed return to normal. It has been clearly demonstrated that several years of tariff stagnation have been very detrimental to Canada. There was the greatest evidence of this during the

period that elapsed from the termination of the Great War to the defeat of Toryism in 1921. The Canadian dollar had depreciated to an alarming extent, an adverse balance of trade was in evidence, Canadians were losing faith in themselves and unity of strength was lacking as between the different elements of our population. This situation, Mr. Speaker, could not be remedied overnight.
It speaks well for this government, that conditions have taken such a decisive and sure return to normal. That the fiscal policy of this government will stimulate this reaction is a foregone conclusion. Surely, Mr. Speaker, no one can deny the fact that the immediate help given to our basic industries by this budget will bring better days to Canada and its people.
It is very interesting to note how easy it is to set the whole political machinery working when an attempt is made to free the common people from the burden of taxation, when such reductions will reflect either directly or indirectly upon the big interests. If hon. members will recollect the campaign launched by the press to defeat reciprocity in 1911, it can very well be stated that the same propaganda is about to be let loose, that the press supporting my friends opposite is ever ready to camouflage the issue in an attempt to mislead the masses of the people.
Already it has been said that manufacturing concerns have had to close their doors as a direct result of a reduction in the import duties. If the reductions suggested in the budget-reductions which are partly upset by a rebate in the cost of raw materials-will force these manufacturers to discontinue their operations, I cannot but infer that these industrials are not imbued with that spirit of courage and determination which should characterize every true Canadian citizen. If our manufacturers cannot loyally and fearlessly put their hands to the wheel and help to alleviate the heavy burdens placed on the shoulders of our people by the extravagant expenditures of the late administration if they cannot forsake some of their profits in order to stimulate business in Canada, if they cannot muster together enough of self control, enough ingenuity, enough of that resourcefulness which we must reasonably expect the business men of this country to possess in order to carry on their business and overcome the obstacles which they profess to find in these tariff reductions-how then can they expect the farmers of the West as well as those of the East, to support the heavy burden which is imposed upon them by customs duties and otherwise? How can they expect
The Budget-Mr. Manion
a man with a family of ten or twelve, such as we so frequently find in the provinces of the East, to subsist on the meagre salary of a bushman or the scant revenue of a small farm, and pay into the pockets of the manufacturer large proportions of their earnings so as to increase the earnings of these latter to such an extent that millions of dollars are now available to wage war against the consumers.
The time is opportune, Mr. Speaker, for the country to grasp the situation with a true sense of Canadian citizenship. Never has the opportunity been so favourable to unite under one policy, under one flag, the destinies of our country; and for this reason and in the fulfilment of my most sacred duties towards my electors and my country it will be my pleasure to give my wholehearted support to the budget.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. J. MANION (Fort William and Rainy River):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I join most
heartily in the expressions of sympathy for the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) in his serious illness, and in the hopes which have been expressed that he may soon be in his seat again. May I at the same time express a word of sympathy with my right hon. leader (Mr. Meighen) who has sustained such a serious affliction within the past few days? My sympathy is all the stronger, Sir, in view of the fact that during the past two months, although a very busy man, I know that he always made time to visit his sick father at least twice or thrice every day.
In looking over the budget which is now before the House, Mr. Speaker, anyone who is at all fair in his estimate must, I submit, after considering its various aspects, come to the conclusion that if the budget is accepted and endorsed by the country at the next election, it is the forerunner of free trade for the Dominion.
Hear, hear.

I hear some applause from hon. members to my left. Therefore apparently they are hoping that this will be the case, and as they are in a position to command they will probably see to it that this result follows. If this budget is accepted and endorsed by the country, it will be a departure from the fiscal policy which Canada has enjoyed from 1878 to 1923. I use the word "enjoyed" advisedly, Sir, because anyone who looks over the statistics showing the progress which this country has made on the whole from 1878 to the present time must be convinced that Canada has had a fair share of prosperity during those years.

The Budget-Mr. Manion
I may be asked in what I base my statement that if this budget is accepted and endorsed by the people it means free trade for Canada. I base my assertion upon two main points. First, upon the slashing cuts in the tariff on many lines of goods which have been made by the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), cuts which, to my mind, are more marked than any which have ever been made in the tariff in any previous budget. Secondly, upon the speeches of those who have preceded m'e in this debate: Upon the speech of my hon. friend the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) in which he, as the first member of the government speaking after the budget was delivered, in a carefully prepared statement, said that he hoped this budget was the death knell of protection in Canada; upon the speech of the hon. minister without portfolio from Prince Edward Island (Mr. Sinclair), who took practically the same attitude; upon the speech of the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Cahill), who congratulated the government on the tariff cuts and hoped that the duty on boots and shoes might be reduced next; upon the speeches of my hon. friends to the left who have rejoiced in the tariff cuts, and have rejoiced also in the hope that further reductions will come in the near future, pointing out that the present reductions were only a beginning. As I stated a minute ago, the Progressive party is in a position of command at the present time; the government cannot retain power without the support of the Progressive party in this House. I say therefore that no party could carry out such a policy as this without the support of my hon. friends to the left. Consequently, being in a position of command, and being sincere in their views in regard to free trade-as I give them credit for-I submit there are very sound grounds for assuming that if this budget is accepted and endorsed by the people it means the beginning of free trade for the Dominion.
At the same time, Sir, there is, I think, great satisfaction in the minds of public men generally that at last this issue is clearly defined. I feel that it is an advantage to the people generally to have this issue defined in such a way that free traders will have to take one side of the political fence and protectionists the other side. No longer will hon. gentlemen like the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond), the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler), the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George (Mr. Marler), the hon. ex-Minister of Justice (Sir

Lomer Gouin) and other hon. gentlemen in the Liberal ranks be able to take the attitude of protection in their own constituencies, knowing that free trade is being preached in other constituencies, but feeling assured that if the party which they are supporting should win no damage would be done to the industrial interests of this country.
Sir, no longer will those who stand for a tariff for revenue be able to say that they hope there will be enough incidental protection to take care of the industries of this country. As a matter of fact a tariff for revenue is not protective at all: it is a false term when used by any hon. gentleman in this House or out of it as indicating in any way a protective tariff. A tariff for revenue is such a tariff as Great Britain has to-day; it is a free trade tariff, if I may use the expression-though it was stated, I remember, by someone in the last election that that was not a proper term. I submit that it is, Sir, because a tariff for revenue means a tariff upon luxuries, which can be imposed under any system, a tariff upon goods which are not produced in the country, as in England they raise five-sixths of their customs revenue from imposts upon sugar, tea and tobacco, which for the most part are not produced in their own country. But if there is any tariff put upon goods which are produced in the country, then a compensating excise duty must be put upon the commodity produced at home in order to take away any element of protection. So that our tariff for revenue men will not be able to claim that they are protectionists.
It must be a source of satisfaction to the people of the country to feel that in the next election they will be able by their voice and vote to say which policy must be accepted and carried out in the Dominion of Canada. No longer will the Liberal-Conservative party be accused of dragging in the free trade bogey by the scruff of the neck, as they have been accused in the past, because the government in power to-day, by their marked cuts in the tariff, by their promises of more to come, and by their expressed hope that this is the death knell of protection, have defined the issue upon which the next election will be fought in this country, and the people will decide the result.	So I believe we may
congratulate ourselves, Mr. Speaker, upon the defining of the issue, upon the fact that we are now at least out in the open, and that the people, not this House, will settle this question finally.
Believing, Sir, in protection as the best policy which Canada can have, believing in

The Budget-Mr. Manion
the dangers not only commercially and economically but nationally to Canada in a policy of free trade, I have no difficulty in taking sides on this question. I find myself happily associated with the group in this House who have since 1878 stood for a protective policy for Canada. Neither will my hon. friends to my left, out and out free traders, as most of them are, have any difficulty in taking sides on this question. But there are a number of hon. gentlemen in the Liberal party who call themselves protectionist Liberals who will have to come out in the open and take sides either for free trade or for protection. So that
5 p.m. the government may be congratulated, in a sense, upon having unconsciously defined the issue, even though they have done so much damage to the industries of this country.
There have been more complaints about this budget than have been offered in respect of any budget previously brought down in Canada. The farm implement manufacturers have complained, the wagon manufacturers, the steel manufacturers, the paint manufacturers-these have complained about what has been done; and the boot and shoe and the woollen manufacturers have complained about what might have been done to help them that has been left undone.
There is one quality in this budget upon which I should like to congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and one quality alone, and that was its brevity, because, Sir, if he did so much damage to the industries of this country in forty minutes I find myself fearing what he could have done had he gone on for an hour and a half. It is said that brevity is the soul of wit. I must confess that I find very little either of wit or of wisdom in this budget. It is a good deal like nitro-glycerine, of which a small amount can cause a great deal of damage: this budget has done more damage in less time than any budget which has ever been produced in Canada. I imagine it was a rather difficult budget for the Acting Minister of Finance to produce, because those of us who have known and liked him for the past seven years or so in this House have looked upon him as one of the outstanding instances of the protectionist on the Liberal side. Of course, I do not suppose any one of us has the right to object to the Acting Minister of Finance standing on his head, but we do object to his standing the whole industrial life of Canada on its head.
Now, Sir, dealing with the budget, I should like to ask what there is in this budget which will do any good to the people. It might be
answered that the cutting down of the sales tax will do good. Well, I am not quarrelling with that; I submit that if the sales tax could be cut off altogether it would probably be for the benefit of Canada. But that is only naturally getting away from taxation as we get away from the war; it has nothing to do with the tariff cuts. And what have the tariff cuts done? I shall give my own opinion, for as much as it is worth, but such as it is I must lay it before the House. The tariff reductions will first of all benefit the United States industries concerned. Secondly, they will injure seriously, if not ruin, the Canadian industries affected, and they will depress all other industries, because no industrial leader knows today when the government will feel it necessary to cut off his head and throw it to the wolves in order that the administration may be kept in power. Thirdly, they will discourage, if not halt, the investment of Canadian money in industrial enterprises, because if there are two things which those require who invest in industrial enterprises, they are security for the present and stability for the future, and there is neither security not stability in this budget. Fourth, they will increase unemployment in Canada; they will drive more of the artisans and workingmen of Canada to the United States and so diminish the home market for the farmers, particularly in Ontario and Quebec. Someone has said, I think it was the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton)-and it was a reasonable statement-that the men who left this country would, had they been employed here, earn an average of about $1,000 per annum each. As we lost 181,000 people last year, even dividing that number by two it means an annual loss to this country of from $100,000,000 to $200,000,000 per annum. In fact, it is one of the greatest exports we have, and I presume that next year this government, which has so little of which to boast and which boasts of so little, may probably boast that they have been the producers of one of the greatest exports in that regard. I notice that this year they included in their exports settlers' effects, the property of those who had permanently left the country.
What are the compensations to the prairie provinces for the destructive features of the budget? The most that any of us, even the most optimistic, could claim would be a reduction of a very few cents in the prices of farm implements bought by the people on the prairies. I submit that it is not the tariff that is injuring the prairie provinces. It is not the tariff which is bringing about a period of stagnation and depression in this

The Budget-Mr. Manion
country-at least, not the high tariff.'In fact, may I interject that under all systems, whether of free trade or protection, in any country we have from time to time periods of depression and stagnation. But the injury to the prairie provinces has really been brought about by four main conditions. First, the world conditions, the chaotic conditions of Europe which have destroyed markets, lessened the purchasing power of the people, and so to a great extent brought about the lowering of the prices of the products of the prairies. Secondly, there is the long haul over which the prairie products have to pass to the seaboard in order that they may be distributed to the markets of the world. Third, as claimed by the people of the prairies themselves, there are the marketing conditions, in respect to which they are proposing different pooling arrangements. Fourth, there is the lack of proper credits for the farmers of the West- that. again is a claim of their own, and I put it forward for what it is worth; they claim there is an intermediate zone of credit which is not looked after. I suppose that any one of these four has a much greater effect upon the depression in the West than any effect that might be brought about by tariffs. The same conditions are injuring the wheat fanners of the prairie states, because they are in very much the same position as our own farmers in the West.
Then what is the object of the changes in the tariff? Sir, it is simply a mad desire on the part of this government to keep in power at any price. It is an attempt to purchase the votes of the West at the expense of the industrial East. Someone has described this budget as national suicide; I should like to describe it as national homicide, because it is a premeditated killing of the industrial East to gain the votes of the West.
It may be said that that language is too strong. Well, in view of the broken pledges of the present government in regard to tariff matters I do not think that the language is too strong. Let me in just a few words review those broken pledges: First, in 1919 there was the platform of the Liberal party under which free trade was proposed in many lines, but the whole was jettisoned as soon as the party got into power. Then, secondly, there was the Prime Minister's promise, quoted the other day in this House by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond), that no legitimate industry would be injured if the Liberal party got into power. Certainly some legitimate industries are being injured at the present time, Then in 1922 there were a few minor cuts in
fMr. Manion.]
the tariff with a promise of more to come, and in 1923 Mr. Fielding, realizing the danger of the course he was pursuing, made a few further cuts but stated that we had gone	far	enough	and	that	stabilitywas needed in this country if we were to have industrial prosperity. Then in 1924, in	the	Speech	from	the	Throne,
we have stability thrown to the winds and promises made of further tariff cuts. Then deputations came down and waited upon the Acting Minister of Finance and the government, and the Acting Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister, according to the press reports, practically promised to those deputations that they need not fear that they were going to be injured from a tariff standpoint at all. I hold in my hand editorials from strong protectionist journals congratulating the government on that attitude. However, only a few weeks later marked cuts in the tariff were announced in the budget. I do not think that a better illustration of confusion worse confounded could be given than the action of the government with respect to the tariff. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the whole tariff history of this government has been one of deception, trickery, and vote chasing. It has been a course of promise and recant, advance and retreat, dodge and sidestep,-in fact it may well be considered a sort of improvised political fox trot: a few steps forward, a few steps back, a sideways glide, and then turn around.
May I, Mr. Speaker, now deal with the question of free trade and protection in this country? The question of whether we shall have free trade or protection in Canada is of the utmost importance to this country. I repeat it is of the utmost importance, not only commercially and industrially but nationally. Not only does our national prosperity depend upon this issue but our national destiny also depends upon it, because in the final analysis the decision whether we are to have free trade or protection in Canada will have a preponderating effect upon our relations not only with the British Isles but with the great republic to the south. Is not that logical? Once we come to depend upon the United States as a market for our raw materials-for our timber, for our fish, for our minerals, and so on-how are we going to maintain that market in anything like a stable manner without some form of union with the United States? Suppose that again in the future, just as at the present time, another high tariff party comes into power in the United States, and they adopt another tariff, just as high as at the present time or

The Budget-Mr. Manion
even higher, against the raw materials and products of Canada, will not this country be placed in a worse position than it is to-day? And how then can we possibly retain anything like trade stability without some form of union with the United States? Sir, the policy of free trade if it were finally brought into operation in this country-as I think it will be if the people endorse the present changes in the tariff-would finally lead to the economic domination of Canada by the United States. It would then lead to Canada becoming a commercial appendage, a commercial adjunct as someone has said, of the United States. It would lead first to commercial union and then to annexation as stated by Mr. Taft and Mr. Champ Clark during the campaign for reciprocity.

Those gentlemen denied
that they made any such statement.

I have their statements
under my hand. I do not know that either of them has denied the statements which were credited to him.
Yes they have.

There are perhaps those in Canada who claim it might be a good thing for Canada from a material standpoint to be joined up with the United States, but I believe that even though it involves some sacrifices the vast majority of the people of Canada prefer to build up" a great Canadian nation on the northern half of this continent. It might be well worth while to draw the prospect that opens before the people of this country to their attention; it might possibly be well worth while to draw that possible outcome to the attention of the people of the province of Quebec. The people of Quebec are probably the most sincerely attached to the British North America Act as it stands to-day. They do not wish to have any greater liberties than they enjoy; they do not wish to have their destinies committed to the care even of a majority of Canadians much less to a majority of Americans. And, Sir, it might be well for them to realize that if we accept free trade in this country we go a long way towards perhaps wiping out not only their industrial prominence in Canada, but also that which they value even more highly than industrial pre-eminence. I think, Sir, that most red-blooded Canadians believe in the building up of a powerful Canadian nation in this Dominion and are willing to make such sacrifices as are necessary to maintain it. They like the American people, I myself like them, but we object to being
swallowed up by them, as we certainly will be if we allow ourselves to become entirely dependent upon the United States as a market for our raw materials and other products.
I have no doubt this attitude will be derided and sneered at by many people in this country, and perhaps by none more strongly than those who hope that prospect may come true.
I should like to give some evidence of the statement I make, I should like to give some reasons-not as a flag-waving proposition at all-why I believe that what I have predicted will ultimately result. Let us look for proof to Cobden. When we discuss the question of free trade in England we naturally think of Cobden, the most outstanding example of a free trade apostle, in the English speaking world at any rate. Cobden's whole life, his eloquence, and his great ability were devoted to advocating free trade in the United Kingdom. His object was that not only should the United Kingdom continue to be a manufacturing country but that ultimately it might become the workshop of the world, that it should be put in such a position that it could dominate the manufacturing markets of the world. He made a statement that is well worth quoting. He said that if England adopted free trade, the whole world would adopt that policy in ten years and he added- and this is the point-"When the whole world has adopted free trade it will dig, delve and plough for England". That was his thought regarding countries that did not go in for manufacturing, for a broader national and industrial life. I submit, Mr. Speaker, that if this budget is accepted by the people of Canada, not only will free trade follow but Canadians will finally be placed in the position where they will dig, delve and plough for the United States. They will become hewers of wood, growers of grain and miners of minerals for the United States, and probably for some of the other industrial countries of the world; and any Canadian of courage, energy, enterprise who wishes to employ those qualities in other lines of industry will have to go to the United States to do so. In other words, such a Canadian will have to expatriate himself from his country and join the exodus of his fellow countrymen from Canada, an exodus which is already far greater than it should be and which will make the Biblical exodus by comparison look like a U.F.O. parade in the city of Toronto at the present time.
There is still another difference between the exodus of old and the exodus of to-day. In the exodus of the Old Testament the children of Israel were led into the land of promise by the wisdom of Moses. In the exodus of to-day the children of Canada are being driven

The Budget-Mr. Manion
into the land of the Stars and Stripes by the voice of Jacob-the Acting Finance Minister.
I shall now deal to a little further extent with the question of protection. There is a tendency in Canada to-day to accuse any one who upholds the policy of protection of being a friend of the "Big Interests." That, Sir, is done in spite of the fact that if you look over the history of tariff legislation throughout the world you will find that the majority of great statesmen supported protection for their different countries, whereas a very small minority of statesmen in the world supported free trade for their countries. Let me just name but a few of the outstanding men the mention of whose names alone suffices to bring them to the recollection of the people of Canada. In the United States there were George Washington, Alexander Hamilton-perhaps the greatest finance minister the United States ever had- Henry Clay, Daniel Webster, Abraham Lincoln, McKinley and Harding to name only a few of them. Of the men that I have mentioned no nobler or more honourable figure ever appeared before the people of the United States or any other nation than Abraham Lincoln. In Great Britain Joseph Chamberlain and Arthur Balfour supported protection. In France that policy was supported by Colbert, who was the great finance minister during the reign of Louis XIV, and by Napoleon; and from 1865 down to the present day all the outstanding statesmen of France have upheld protection for that country. In Germany, Frederick the Great and Bismarck were supporters of protection, and all German statesmen down to the present day have continued to be protectionists. In Canada we had Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Wilfrid Laurier. As to the latter statesman I make this statement: Notwithstanding any quotations that can be brought forward from the speeches of Sir Wilfrid Laurier he never made any move to introduce free trade into Canada.
Reciprocity which the hon. member supported.

Reciprocity, Mr. Speaker,
was based on protection. Reciprocity was based upon the very fact that you have protection in this countiy. It was an exchange of favours with the United States. The United States was giving us favours in return for favours which we gave them. It was a reciprocal arrangement, and could not be carried out by any other than a protective country. Great Britain could not have reciprocity with any other country because she has free trade. Neither could we have reciprocity with any country if we were free traders. In addition to the fact that these men whom I have named, 
who are outstanding men in the history of the world, were all protectionists, there is the fact that all the countries of the world of any importance have prospered under protection, Let me mention a few of them. France before the war was one of the richest countries in the world, a country in which the wealth was more evenly divided than in any other country in the world. The agricultural and industrial life was more evenly balanced than in any other country, and it has had marked protection for over a hundred years, but certainly has had high protection from the year 1865. Germany, from the time of Bismarck in 1870, till the present time, was a highly protected country, and before the wrar she was not only rapidly catching up to Great Britain in many lines, but had surpassed her in some lines. She was selling more goods to most of the countries in Europe; and if she had had sense enough not to start the war, but to continue along peaceful lines, she would be probably the greatest commercial country in the world. The United' States has been a highly protected country since 1861. Previous to that time the United States tried the principle of free trade three times, and on all occasions that trial was succeeded by times of panic, depression and stagnation. Since 1861 the United States has had a continuous period of protection, and I make the statement that in general prosperity, in developed natural resources and in the real wages and social conditions of the people and opportunities of life, the United States has been the most outstanding nation by long odds of any country in the world.
I have stated that all countries have built up their prosperity upon a foundation of protection. I some time ago made that statement in regard to Great Britain, and many hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House took occasion to differ with me. I wish to give two proofs very briefly of my statement that England built up her prosperity upon a protective foundation. I hold in my hand Macaulay's History of England, Volume 1. This history was published for the first time in 1848. It is a voluminous work, and there is a number of volumes. It must have taken Macaulay some years to prepare it. But he makes comparison in the third chapter, which I have here marked between conditions in England in 1685 and 1845, a period of 150 years. That would be rather a long period for Canada, but would not be a long period for England, because she has a thousand years of history behind her. I do not intend to read very much, though the whole chapter deals with a comparison of these different

The Budget-Mr. Manion
periods, and bears out what I have stated, but I will read a few sentences:
Younger towns, towns which are rarely or never mentioned in our early history and which sent no representatives to our early parliaments, have, within the memory of persons, still living, grown to a greatness which this generation contemplates with wonder and pride, not unaccompanied by awe and anxiety.
The most eminent of these towns were indeed known in the seventeenth century as respectable seats of industry. Nay, their rapid progress and their vast opulence were then sometimes described in language which seems ludicrous to a man who has seen their present grandeur. One of the most populous and prosperous among them was Manchester.
Speaking of the cotton trade of Manchester, he says:
The whole annual import did not, at the end of the seventeenth century, amount to two millions of pounds, a quantity which would now hardly supply the demand of forty-eight hours.
He is making a comparison between the end of the seventeenth century and 1845.
That wonderful emporium, which in population and wealth far surpasses capitals so much renowned as Berlin, Madrid and Lisbon, was then a mean and ill-built market town, containing under six thousand people. It then had not a single press. It now supports a hundred printing establishments. It then had not a single coach. It now supports twenty coach-makers.
Leeds was already the chief seat of the woolen manufacturers of Yorkshire... But from the returns of the hearth money it seems certain that the whole population of the borough, an extensive district which contains many hamlets, did not, in the reign of Charles the Second, exceed seven thousand souls. In 1841 there were more than a hundred and fifty thousand.
About a day's journey south of Leeds, on the verge of a wild moorland tract, lay an ancient manor, now rich with cultivation, then barren and unenclosed, which was known by the name of Hallamshire. Iron abounded there... It had indeed been mentioned by Geoffrey Chaucer in one of his Canterbury Tales. But the manufacture appears to have made little progress during the three centuries which followed his time.
Most of the Hallamshire forges were collected in a market town which had sprung up near the castle of the proprietor, and, which, in the reign of James the First, had been a singularly miserable place, containing about two thousand inhabitants, of whom a third were half starved and half naked beggars... This is that Sheffeld which now, with its dependencies, contains a hundred and twenty thousand souls, and which sends forth its admirable knives, razors and lancets to the farthest ends of the world.
Birmingham had not been thought of sufficient importance to return a member to Oliver's parliament... Yet in 1685 the population, which is now little less than two hundred thousand, did not amount to four thousand.
These four chief seats of our great manufactures deserve especial mention. It would be tedious to enumerate all the populous and opulent hives of industry which a hundred and fifty years ago, were hamlets without parish churches, or desolate moors inhabited only by grouse and wild deer.
Liverpool contains more than three hundred thousand inhabitants.
And he gives the population of the time which he is comparing it with as four thousand. Then he says:
Into her custom house has been repeatedly paid in one year a sum more than twice as great as the whole income of the English Crown in 1685.
Her endless docks, quays and warehouses are among the wonders of the world.
Further on he says, speaking of London:-
