English writers boasted of the forest of masts and yardarms which covered the river from the Bridge to the Tower, and of the stupendous sums which were collected at the Custom House in Thames street... Yet to our generation the honest vaunting of our ancestors must appear almost ludicrous. The shipping which they thought incredibly great appears not to have exceeded seventy thousand tons. This was, indeed, then more than a third of the whole tonnage of the Kingdom, but is now less than a fourth of the tonnage of Newcastle, and is nearly equalled by the tonnage of the steam vessels of the Thames. The customs of London amounted in 1685, to about three hundred and thirty thousand pounds a year. In our time the net duty paid annually, at the same place, exceeds ten millions.
That is sufficient to show Macaulay's views of the conditions of Great Britain for the 150 years between 1685 and 1845, before free trade was adopted in Great Britain.
I will give one more quotation, and this is from Joseph Chamberlain. He made speeches, as hon. members all km w, in which he stated that he believed in a preference. In other words he believed in protection for England, and here are two very brief quotations from two of his speeches. At Birmingham on November 4, 1903 he said:
If it were true that protection inevitably brought with it destitution, misery and starvation, and free trade brought with it prosperity and progress, how do you account for the fact that every foreign country without exception that has adopted protection has in recent years at any rate progressed more rapidly and in greated proportion than we, the free trade country of the world.
And he points out that the once great British trade in sugar refining has gone; the iron trade is going; and the cotton trade is threatened. At Newcastle two years later he said further: Whereas in the five and twenty years after Mr. Cobden's great reform was carried, this country was an industrial centre exchanging its manufactures with other countries for their food and raw materials. Now we have ceased to hold any such position of industrial supremacy; we are daily sending out more raw materials and coal, and importing more foreign manufactured goods; that is, we are importing more and more of those goods which give the greatest employment to the working classes.
I think in view of those two opinions-and I could quote many more if I wished to-
The hon. member knows the answer the people of England gave to Chamberlain?

Yes, and I think I know the answer the people of Canada will give to the present government. In view of these two opinions and quotations which I have read
to the House, I think I am basing my remarks

I was informed that a good many of those industries my hon. friend speaks about, were not able to compete with other Canadian industries, at Brantford, for instance. I was informed that particularly at Port Arthur large works were put up that could not carry on business because they were not able to compete with Canadian industries, not United States industries. I may be wrong.

My hon. friend is wrong.
I am not speaking of any industry that was built that was not competing.
My hon. friend admits that some buildings were erected that were not operating?

Yes, but I did not mention them. There were some plants which were built at the head of the lakes which were never occupied. But I mentioned one plant which prior to a couple of years ago employed 300 persons at Fort William. I mentioned another, which usually employs about 300 people and which is now operating with about 60. The third plant operated, to my recollection, prior to two years ago or, at most, three years ago, not to its full extent, but it did employ about 1,000 people, and it is now closed down. It was regarding this plant that I read from the last letter which I quoted. Those are industries only in my constituency. There are throughout this country many other plants of various lines which are being hit by this budget and by the danger of having their tariff protection cut. We all know about the agricultural implement industry, the steel industry, which is hit in this budget, the paint industry, and some of the paint manufacturers stated in Montreal the other day that they would
The Budget-Mr. Manwn
have to close down absolutely. There is also the boot and shoe industry and the woollen industry. The boot and shoe industry employed about 14,000 people in this country and to-day it is operating at about 60 per cent of its capacity. The woollen and knitted goods industry employed about 22,000 to 23,000 people and it is now operating today at about 40 per cent of its capacity.

Has the boot and shoe
men's employment decreased since the budget has been brought down?

I am blaming their being
closed down on the fact that the country is being inundated with British goods and French goods, particularly British goods in the case of boots and shoes, and they have not the protection they require which the budget should have given. Last year some cuts were made in the preferential tariff which did hurt the boot and shoe manufacturers. At any rate the boot and shoe manufacturers need greater protection if they are to compete against the low labour costs and the depreciated exchange of Europe, and they cannot continue with the tariff which they have at present in Canada.
What about those factories that closed down two or three years ago when the late government was in office or shortly after the present government came in?

I would criticise exactly in the same way. If they required increased tariff protection to keep them going, I say they should have had it. I do not know if any closed down three years ago. In 1923 some $40,000,000 worth of woollen and knitted goods was imported into this country.
I am taking that from the records of this government. Just think what it would mean to the people engaged in those industries if that amount was produced in Canada. It is true that the hon. member for Brome (Mr. McMaster) said the other day that you could not increase employment in a country by protection; all you do if you close up one industry is you simply drive a man into a more remunerative industry. But the trouble is that we are driving them into more remunerative industries in the United States. This is another case of the theory and the fact not agreeing. I have noticed with free traders that if the facts disagree with the theory, it is so much the worse for the facts.
Even the Toronto Globe took, and has been taking, the attitude-I have a number

The Budget-Mr. Manion
of its editorials in my possession-in regard to the woollen and knitted goods industry that they are not receiving the proper care and attention that they should be receiving. I submit that the boot and shoe industry and the woollen and knitted goods industry should get the protection which they need to keep them going.
One of our Progressive friends, speaking on this very question in a recent debate, said something to this effect: "Your Protectionists say that your industries cannot compete with those in France, in England, and in the United States". Then, quite dramatically, he asked: "What in heaven's name can they compete with!" Well, Mr. Speaker, there is a simple answer to that question: they can compete with one another; and that is all that any other country would ask their manufacturers to do in the way of competition.
Oh, oh.

My hon. friends no doubt are laughing at the fact that there is serious unemploj'ment in this country at the present time. But let me assure them that this unemployment is due to that very fact, that our industries are forced to compete with those outside the country. There are nearly two million people out of employment in Great Britain, and the fact must be significant to hon. gentlemen that, where this enormous unemployment exists, the industries are forced to compete with foreign manufacturers. Indeed!, Mr. Speaker, there is no country in the world that I know of that is in so pitiable a condition, from the point of view of unemployment, as the United Kingdom, which is the only free trade nation at the present time. Now, I do not know why we should make such frantic efforts to defend our national freedom when it is threatened by invading troops, and at the same time neglect our commercial freedom when it is menaced by industrial forces that are equally dangerous. And yet that is just the situation to-day.
Look back over the history of the world and you will find that those countries which have lived a broad national life and have carried on a wide and diversified industrial development, are the countries which have been best able to take care of themselves. Look at the United States at the time of the Civil War. What does history reveal in that case? Why, we find that the South was defeated mainly by reason of the fact that, unlike the North, it had no industrial development, From the very beginning it was realised that the South must lose eventually because it could not produce the goods which it needed. Again, take the example we have in the

recent war. Why were Great Britain, the United States and France able to subdue Germany ? . They could do so only because they had had a wide and a marked industrial development. Without that development they would have been beaten, as surely as I am standing here to-day. And as a matter of fact, Sir, Germany herself was able to ward off defeat for a period of four years simply because she had magificently developed herself industrially under a policy of protection.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Was she not the best equipped industrially?

Yes, but she had the whole world against her. Of course she was well equipped industrially, and that is precisely why it took four and a half years for the Allies to subdue her. Had she not been as well equipped as she was she must have succumbed within a year. Now, Sir, if this budget is accepted and endorsed by the people of Canada we shall declare ourselves to be, apart from Great Britain, the only nation that despises that strength and independence with which other countries have developed industrially by means of protection. England is the only free trade country in the world, and if we adopt this budget we shall be the second; in other words we shall be virtually proposing to fall into that state which Russia was in before she decided to adopt protection one hundred years ago.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: Surely my hon. friend would not assert that England could not play her part in the war.

No, I do not say that, nor have I said anything of the kind. I showed earlier in my remarks that England had built up the foundation for her industrial life and prosperity upon the basis of protection up to the year 1846.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext: The question I asked my hon. friend was, whether he would make the statement that England could not play her part in the war.

Not at all. We over on this side are always accused of flag-waving, but it seems that a little of this is being done on the other side now. My hon. friend is trying to make me say that England did not play her part in the war. Of course, I know otherwise.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
speechtext:
I had no such thought. I do not want to interject any remarks into my hon. friend's speech, but he argues that protectionist countries have been better able to protect themselves than free trade countries. I hope he will not accuse me of waving the flag; I never do that.

The Budget-Mr. Manion
Are we not entitled to do a little of the waving at times over here? Some of the rest of us did our part in the war too.

I am not denying that
for a moment; and I wish that hon. gentlemen opposite, and to my left, would wave the Canadian flag a little more.

It is not always those
who wave the flag that are the most patriotic.	.

I do not know that you
can necessarily prove that. I was about to observe, when I was so generally interrupted, that even those men who have had world wide reputations as advocates of free trade have admitted the necessity in some cases for a policy of protection. Let me put on Hansard a quotation from John Stuart Mill, who was a more outstanding free trader than even my hon. friend from Brome (Mr. Mc-Master) or for that matter any other hon. gentleman in this House. The following statement by Mill is worth considering:
The superiority of one country over another in a branch of industry often arises only from its having begun sooner. A country which has this skill and experience to acquire may in other respects be better adapted to production than those earlier in the field; and, besides, it is a just remark that nothing has a greater tendency to produce improvement in any branch of production than its trial under a new set of conditions. But it cannot be expected that individuals should at their own risk, or rather to their certain loss, introduce a new manufacture and bear the burthen of carrying it on until the producers have been educated up to the level of those with whom the processes have become traditional. A protecting duty continued for a reasonable time will sometimes be the least inconvenient mode in which a country can tax itself for the support of such an experiment.
And we have had protection for sixty years.

Yes, and I submit that
we have been doing well under it, even though my hon. friend thought it necessary to declare recently that he was sick and tired of the policy. I do not wish to burden Hansard again with the figures that I have already given, but I can submit to hon. gentlemen the facts that prove that we have had prosperity in Canada and that it was built up on protection. It is quite true that ^.t the present time Canada is suffering; but-she is suffering a period of depression which is common to the whole world, with the exception of the United States, which is the most highly protected country we know of to-day.
In the closing years of John Stuart Mill's life he was asked by Mr. Geo. W. Smalley, of the New York Tribune, whether he still 99
adhered to the statement which he had made as quoted by me a moment ago. He replied:
Certainly; I have never affirmed anything to the contrary. I do not presume to say that the United States may not find protection expedient in their present state of development. I do not even say that, if I were an American I should not be a protectionist.
So that even John Stuart Mill who was perhaps the most outstanding free trader of his time, admitted that protection was advisable in many cases. If one cared to do so one could cite many industries in the United States which have been built up exclusively under protection. I might mention, for example, the tin plate industry- and there are many others-which did not exist in the United States, except to a very minor degree, until 1890. Up to that time it produced annually about two million pounds of tin plate; but under protection, introduced in 1890, it immediately developed until it produced 2,000,000,000 pounds, sweeping the Welsh tin plate industry off its feet and driving the tin plate workers of Wales into the United States factories. I could cite many other industries which have similarly developed under protection, but I do not wish to take up the time of the House further.
Now, in the final analysis, what is the real object of those who demand free trade? I think I can state it in a single word-cheapness. Cheapness of goods is the sole object of this cry for free trade; and I remember our good friend Dr. Michael Clark, who came from the constituency now represented in this House by my hon. friend from Red Deer (Mr. Speakman), saying on one occasion:	"We want cheap goods, and we
care not whence they come". That after all is the basis of the free trade argument: cheapness of goods is the sole reason. In other words, we are asked to sacrifice the industrial East in order that the prairie provinces may save a few cents on farm implements and boots and shoes. I say that without the slightest intention of offending the prairie provinces, but simply because it is from that section of the country that the cry comes for free trade. It is debatable whether we shall get cheaper goods under free trade. However, merely for the sake of argument, let us admit that we shall. In that case, is the cheapness worth the sacrifice that we shall make? Is not a diversified national development, a broad national life, the greatest objective at which we could aim? Is it not worth striving for to bring about such conditions as shall prevent our youth from going to the United States? Is not that state of affairs worth something to

The Budget-Mr. Manion

the Canadian people? Why should cheapness of goods be worshipped as a god? It is much more desirable that we should provide employment and wages for our Canadian people. I submit that the progress, the prosperity, and the happiness of our people depend very much more upon their ability to earn wages and consequently to purchase goods than upon the opportunity to buy those goods a little cheaper. If you will show me a cheap country, Mr. Speaker, I will show you in return a poor country. Cheap goods are of no use to anybody unless he has the money with which to buy them. I well remember quoting in this House some sessions ago the old story of an Irishman who complained of the fact that he had to pay fifty cents in New York for something which he could get for a shilling in Ireland. He was asked, "Why didn't you buy it in Ireland?" He replied, "I didn't have a shilling." That is the condition in every cheap country. The United States for the past fifty years has probably been the dearest country in the world, and yet it has been the Mecca of all the people of all the cheap countries in the world.
There is no better test of the condition of cheapness in a countiy than the labour cost test. I may be permitted, perhaps, to give two or three experiences of my own with regard to such tests in other countries. I remember before the war being driven around the city of Naples in a cab for a whole afternoon and paying two lire for the accommodation-forty cents at that time. Naples was then one of the cheapest cities I was ever in-and also one of the most poverty-ridden. Let me instance Ireland for the benefit of my hon. friend from Springfield (Mr. Hoey). I remember taking a tour, at least twenty years ago, through the famous lakes of Killarney. I hired a horse-it was really a pony-to go through the gap of Dunloe. For the use of this animal for a whole afternoon I paid half a crown-sixty cents. I asked the man in charge of the horse, "How much do you get out of this?" He answered, "I get whatever you choose to give me as a tip." He was working for the owner of the horse. I said to him, "Why don't you come out to a prosperous country like Canada?" He replied, " It would take me fifteen years to earn enough money to pay my fare to your country." I remember with pain-because Ireland is also the home of my forefathers-that not only in the country districts did beggars hold out their hands for alms, but right in the city of Dublin the poverty was something pitiable. I remember in the same trip that in the native

land of my hon. friend from Brandon (Mr. Forke) at Edinburgh and Glasgow-particularly Edinburgh-poverty was just as marked in the slums there as I observed it in those of London; and I need not particularize the poverty there. In those parts of the British Isles labour was cheap and the cost of living low; but, Sir, at that time, according to a statement made by the late Campbell-Bannerman during the British general election in 1904, thirteen million of the population were on the verge of hunger-and he was a free trader.

Does my hon. friend deny
the fact that in every large manufacturing centre of the world you will find slums and poverty?

No, I do not deny that,
but I make this statement, and I submit that it cannot be- disproved:	There were at that
time more slums and poverty in the British Isles than in the protectionist countries of France, Germany or the United States. I could easily prove this statement By the figures which I put on Hansard a few sessions ago when debating the same question of free trade versus protection, but I do not wish to take up the time of the House now by repeating the figures, and I have not got them at hand.

Does not my hon. friend
agree that the landlord system in Great Britain, the twin brother of protection, is largely responsible for the poverty there?

I do not accept my hon.
friend's statement in its entirety, although I think that system has had something to do with the poverty. I remember reading a book by the late Earl of Dunraven-who lived all his life in Ireland and must be accepted as a better authority respecting conditions in that country than my hon. friend can be-in which he said that the poverty of Ireland was caused by free trade, which had ruined industry and driven out the business of grain growing.

The enormous land rents
were responsible.

They would accentuate
the trouble, of course. I may mention two other countries, India and China, where you may hire labour for a few cents a day and those countries are mainly agricultural. Every few years millions of people in those countries die of famine and disease. In other words, in all cheap countries the people are trying to get out of them as if threatened by a frightful epidemic of some plague. And

The Budget-Mr. Manion
where are they trying to go to-cheaper countries? No, to the dearest country of all, and the most highly protected-the United States. So much so, that the American government, as we all know, has had to put in force a quota law to restrict immigration from those cheap countries.
Again, I submit that what Canada needs is employment for her people-work and wages for her artisans and mechanics. We all deplore the exodus of our young men to the United States. Will anyone tell me that these young men are leaving because of the high cost of living here? Certainly not. Everyone of them is migrating because he has not got work and wages at home. I submit that this budget will lessen work and wages, and so restrict the purchasing power of our artisans and mechanics. In a word, it means for them an empty pocket instead of a full dinner pail; emigration instead of occupation.
Suppose we do get free trade and so cut down the price of goods, will the resultant cheapness which is so much desired continue here? I do not think it will last very long. Aside from the argument-which I think is quite sound-that once the American industrialists have secured control of our markets they will begin to recoup themselves by charging higher prices for their goods, who will pay the main proportion of our taxes? I repeat, I do not mean anything offensive to the farmers in these comparisons which I am making. But who will pay the main proportion of our taxes? There is a tendency on the part of many of my friends from the prairie provinces to take the attitude that they are making all the sacrifices by reason of the tariff duties which they have to pay. I have heard them declare: Let the protectionists get off our backs. That is the attitude which our friends frequently take. I do not admit that all the sacrifices are made by the farmers of the West or by those of any other part of the Dominion. I submit that many sacrifices are made, and made willingly, by the people of our cities and towns. Who pays the bulk of the income tax? Less than 2 per cent of the fifty or sixty millions collected, according to the statement of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), is paid by the rural districts; over 98 per cent, is being paid by the industrial centres.

Why talk so much about
sacrifices when everything is all right in the industrial centres?

I am talking about my
friends to my left claiming that they are making all the sacrifices.
99i
Excuse me, you referred to other people making sacrifices.
So they do. If my hon. friend and his associates are correct in claiming that they are making sacrifices, I am pointing out that the people of the East are making sacrifices too.
We admit the sacrifices; you do not.

I am pointing out the
sacrifices that are being made by the East in regard to other things than the tariff sacrifices that the West complain of.
That is different.

I was referring to the income tax. Let me point out also that, although it is difficult to prove, I may venture to assert that 75 per cent-yes, very much more than 75 per cent, of the customs duties are paid by the cities and towns on the luxuries which they buy.
That is right.
If my hon. friend admits that that is right, then he must admit also that the cities and towns are paying more than their share of taxation.
We admit that they have the luxuries.

Surely my hon. friend does not want to change the whole system of this country whereby men are rewarded for their enterprise and business ability? If so, he is getting back to a proposition coming from Russia with which I do not agree. Not only do the cities and towns pay the bulk of the customs duties and income tax, but they help to pay for rural education, rural roads and rural mail delivery. I have in my constituency rural mail deliveries which do not bring in enough to pay the cost, and there are very many throughout the country. I have pointed out before, but my hon. friends are apt to forget it, that nearly $6,000,000 is given annually by way of direct assistance to the agricultural interests of this country in the estimates before the House. I wish to repeat, because my hon. friend is apparently taking offence at these comparisons-
No.

I wish to repeat that I
am offering no criticism of these conditions. I simply make the statement that if the industrial centres of the East are willing, as they are, to make sacrifices on behalf of the prairie sections of the Dominion, those prairie sections must not expect to make no sacrifices
The Budget-Mr. Manion

at all. If the industrial centres are largely wiped out, who is going to pay the large obligations of this country? Who is going to build , the Hudson Bay railway, which is demanded from the West? Who is going to pay the increased deficits on the Canadian National because of the traffic being to a greater extent north and south than east and west? The West is going to pay a greater proportion than she does now, if she is able, and I submit that the last condition of the West might well be worse than the first. It might be well for the people of the prairie provinces who demand free trade-and I do not need to look always to my left; I may look across the way sometimes-to remember that maxim of Shakespeare, which suggests that we should-
-rather bear those ills we have,
Than fly to others that we know not of.
I fully realize that there is a depression in the West. I fully realize that relief is needed, so far as possible, but I am not admitting that we should wipe out the industrial East to bring about that relief. I repeat that the tariff is not the cause of the present conditions of the West. I have been in surgery for about twenty years and I have never yet seen an opportunity to save a man's arms by amputating his legs, nor do I think that you can save the agricultural arms of this country by amputating its industrial legs.

Sometimes you save a
man's life by cutting off his leg.
Mr. MANION': Apparently my hon. friend and his government are attempting to do that in this country at the present time. For myself I do not think it can occur in fiscal matters.
The hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) in his speech the other day pointed out that we who support protection do not realize the importance of the West to Canada. We do realize the importance of the West to Canada. I realize the importance of all sections-of British Columbia, of the prairie provinces, of the Maritime provinces, and I also realize what he and his friends do not seem to realize, the importance of Ontario and Quebec. I do not know whether I should admit that the two million people in the prairie provinces are more important to Canada than the six million in Quebec and Ontario. I submit that some remedy should be worked out whereby we can help the prairie West, and I am entirely for doing that so far as it is possible, but not to the extent of running some other section of the country.

Protection is needed in the East because of the low labour costs in Europe. One instance of that occurred a few weeks ago when there was a strike in Manchester-at least, it was so reported in the press-the operatives of certain cotton mills there demanding to be paid $7.92, not per day, but per week. Those who were running the mills said that the most they could pay aftd compete witji the rest of the world was $7.04 a week, while for the same line of work in Canada they are paying from $15 to $20 a week. This instance will illustrate the cost of labour in Europe. Then, there is the question of depreciated currency. I hold under my hand.-I shall not take time to read it-a statement by Professor H. Mitchell, of McMaster University, Toronto, in which he points out what everybody knows well who has given any study to the question, that due to the depreciated exchange of Europe there is an invisible bounty paid on the exports of Europe when they come to the United States or Canada. One of the ways that the government could help the industries of Canada would be to protect them against that invisible bounty. In passing, I suggest that in view of the facility with which this government changes its mind overnight, I should not be at all surprised if they brought in some modification of their resolutions to this end, and I hope they do, for the good of the country. At present, however, there is nothing in the budget to protect us against that depreciated exchange which, according to Professor Mitchell and other authorities, owing to the depreciation in the value of the pound sterling, gives from 7 to 10 per cent less protection to the industries of Canada.
Then, there are the handicaps to industry in Canada, the eight-hour day in many provinces; factory laws; workmen's compensation, and standards of living which are higher in Canada even than in such countries as England. In other words, if, as the labour people state, we permit the cheap products of cheap labour to come into this country free, we will deprive our own working people of employment and drive them to the United States. I believe we must help the prairie West. We must do everything we can which does not go to the extent of ruining the industrial East. A national policy for this country is one which should so far as possible help all classes, agriculturists, artisans and industrialists. I admit that it is very difficult to do anything in the line of protection to help my friends of the prairie provinces who grow wheat; I admit that very freely, I admit also that probably they would gain to a certain extent, temporarily, from free trade. But,

The Budget-Mr. Hodgins
Sir, if we cannot help them by protection, then it is our duty to help them in some other way to make up for the sacrifices which I admit they make to a certain extent through the operation of the protective tariff. But we can help the other farmers of this country: we can help the truck farmers, the fruit farmers, the dairy and poultry farmers. Tens of millions of dollars' worth of fruits, vegetables, butter, eggs and cheese are imported into this country to compete with our own products. Let us keep our Canadian markets, not only the industrial markets but the agricultural markets, for our own Canadian people. The Canadian duties to-day on the agricultural products which I have just mentioned are about half the American duties against similar products entering the United States from Canada. Under a proper national policy for this country agriculture and industry could progress and prosper hand in hand, as they should progress and prosper. That Sir, should be the goal of national greatness to which we should aspire; that is the goal to which we will attain if. in the words of Lord Chatham, on another occasion, "we have no craven fear of being great" in this country.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

I desire to occupy a few minutes in expressing my views concerning matters which have been brought forward in the budget, and I can assure hon. members that I shall not speak at undue length. First let me extend my congratulations to the Acting Minister of Finance on the concise and businesslike character of his financial statement. I also desire to sympathize with the Minister of Finance upon his illness, and with the leader of the opposition in the loss which he has just sustained.
As to the budget itself I am in perfect accord with some of the criticisms which have been made. I believe that the surplus for which credit has been claimed is largely a matter of bookkeeping. But the tariff changes which the budget makes undoubtedly create a line of cleavage between the protectionist and the free trader in.this country. I believe with the previous speaker that the budget has brought the issue of protection versus free trade before the country in a way it has never been brought before. When one studies world history one cannot fail to be impressed with certain peculiar features which have attended
the development of this issue. For example the farmers in England to-day are asking for protection while the people who want free trade are the manufacturers. In the United States a few generations ago the farmers were the free traders and the manufacturers were the protectionists. To-day the reverse is the case: The farmers are the protectionists and the manufacturer, or to be quite accurate, the big financial interests of the country, are commencing to clamour for free trade. And why are they doing so. Because they find that in order to market their own products they must trade with foreign countries, and there must be a lowering of the high tariff duties before the products of other countries can secure admission to the United States market. International trade is not trade between nations as nations. What it means is that individuals or firms of a particular nation trade with individuals or firms of other nations. As it appears to me customs duties are simply fines placed upon individuals in return for the privilege of trading with individuals of other countries. If we were to place such fines upon individuals trading with each other in our own country we should look upon it as a very absurd proposition to say the least. But because the other party to the arrangement happens to live in another country the system of imposing fines is regarded as quite proper. But if fines are levied on transactions between different countries why not carry the principle to its logical conclusion and impose duties in the case of transactions between different counties or different provinces of the same country?
If we take the experience of reciprocity in the past doubtless thousands of residents of the United States opposed reciprocity with Canada because they thought it would be profitable to Canadians. Probably, too, reciprocity was opposed by many Canadians because they thought the United States rather than Canada would benefit from that pact. But even if the other country is going to benefit to some degree why should that be disadvantageous to Canada? Under free trade the labour and capital of our country would be forced out of artificial channels and into occupations which would produce with greater efficiency, those articles which we need most. It follows then that if we attain the best results by our tariff policy we shall attract more immigrants and more capital to the country. Then instead of admitting immigrants into Canada indiscriminately we should be able to cull our future citizens from the immigrants that offer and let into the Dominion only the very best.
The Budget-Mr. Hodgins

Taking the four great fundamental industries of our country from which we really derive all our wealth, namely fishing, mining, lumbering and farming, which policy, protection or free trade, will prove the more beneficial to them? If we take the products of those four industries and ask ourselves how much protection has increased the selling price of them, we will have to admit that it is very little, if any. Then we take the materials we have to buy and ask ourselves how much protection has increased the price to us, and in almost every case we must admit it has done so to a considerable extent. We cannot help but realize that protection is far from being a benefit to the people of this or any other country. If it is necessary -and I do not believe it is-to have a protective tariff to enable the manufacturers in this country to live and carry on, we should also have a protective tariff to enable the farmers to live and carry on, and as it is an impossibility to protect the farmer in the greater amount of his products, as he must look outside our country for his market, we should, to place him on an equal footing, grant him a bonus on every bushel of wheat, every pound of beef, every pound of pork and a great many other articles which he produces at the present time. If our protectionist friends wish to come across with a proposition of this kind, they might hope to get some support from the farmer, but I think the foolishness of this is quite evident to them, and I cannot see why they should not be sensible about the tariff arrangements, and be manly enough to stand on their own feet and not to resort to a legalized form of robbery in order to carry on their business. One might just as well allow a merchant in this city who is not making' a profit in his business to come down the street and rob a fellow merchant who is not making any more profit than he himself is making.
Reductions have been made in this budget along some lines, but I believe it is just as necessary and perhaps more so, that reductions should be made all along the line. Taking our boot and shoe industry, there is no reason that I can see why it should be protected to the extent of thirty per cent and other businesses have little or no protection. Building is cheaper in Canada than in the United States. The workers in these factories do not receive as large a wage as in the United States. The machinery which is necessary in these factories is put into the factories in the United States and Canada by the same company and on the same terms; the lasts which are necessary are made from Canadian wood which is right at hand, and 
they have the advantage in freight rates on account of being closer to the Canadian consumer. With all these advantages there is no reason why they should need this protection, and it is the same practically with all the other manufacturing interests. Every other manufacturing business in this country I think would come pretty nearly into the same category. We find to-day a paper company selling paper in the United States cheaper than in Canada and doing so on account of the protection it enjoys, and yet we find the president of the same paper concern going up and down this country preaching the fostering of home industries. It seems to me that that is not exercising very good judgment and is not a consistent policy. If it is necessary that we should retain our custom duties in order that we might raise our revenue, I might suggest to the minister that he place an excise tariff which would be almost if not altogether equal to the present customs tariff, and thereby the country would get the revenue which is at present going into the pockets of the manufacturers; but I would also suggest to the minister that he could collect more money and collect it easier and cheaper by placing a direct tax on the assessed value of the different businesses and occupations throughout the land. I have in my hand a clipping from the California Farmer which says:
All that the farmer can hope to demand is fair play, the removal of unequal burdens, with free access to the markets of the world.
And I might say that that is all we want.
This he will not get at once from any political party, but in proportion to his recognition of his real needs, he can compel their alarmed attention. The prosperity of the few, in which half the nation does not share, is built on sand, and cannot be stable until the farmer comes into his own.

The tariff of the country is a subject of the greatest controversy and this to a large extent is true of almost every country in the world. The budget in this country and the tariff in the country to the south of us have until very recently been subjects of very great controversy. In the years 1919, 1920 and 1921 we had the strongest evidence of antipathy between the then government and the little group in the far-off corner. Very hard words were spoken in those years. And if the group has grown to its present magnitude, it is on account of the fact that the opposition to the government in 1911 fought desperately against reciprocity in natural products, which had been advocated since the abrogation of the reciprocity treaty with the United States in 1865. The emissaries of this country were

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
often in Washington trying to renew that treaty. Prominent men of the day, including Sir John A. Macdonald and members of his cabinet, travelled throughout the country and advocated the renewal of the reciprocity treaty. When the time came that President Taft made overtures to this country to renew that treaty, desperate means were taken to defeat it. The acting leader of the Progressives (Mr. Johnston) the other day made a positive statement in regard to it, and I have not the least doubt that what he said was true, that when the Right Hon. W. S. Fielding went to the great metropolis of Montreal in 1911 and told the interests there that they would make a mistake by turning down reciprocity the result was that they fought desperately against it and contributed freely to the campaign funds to be used against the proposition to adopt that treaty. That caused the defeat of the reciprocity measure.
We should remember that about two-thirds of this great country lies to the west of the province of Ontario, and that for the last two sessions the members of the Progressive party have spent a great deal of time and energy in this House advocating such a measure. They have continued to debate for two sessions with their very extensive vocabulary, and with the full force of their personality, and individuality, and I hope their vocabulary is not larger than their hearts. But this country had come to the point where somebody needed to strike out boldly and endeavour to ascertain if anything could be done in this country, by give and take, to make Canada a country worth living in, where the people would be united, with a tariff that would do the greatest good to the greatest number.
I am glad that we have an Acting Minister of Finance who has proclaimed many times in the past six years that he would not destroy any industry in this country. In other words, he might be considered a protectionist, as I am. I represent a very large industrial community as well as an agricultural community, but I recognize the fact that something must be done in Canada. I was out in my constituency during the last few days and I heard no criticism. On my return I stayed in Montreal for a day and I heard some criticism. As I diagnosed the situation, as nearly as I can find out, the criticism all came from the Manufacturers Association of Canada. Personally, I am a manufacturer. I am identified with many industries as well as a number of businesses. Nearly every dollar that I have is invested, either directly or indirectly in the great industries of this country, so that I would not do and
I should not support anything in the shape of class legislation. We cannot continue in the same way as we have been doing, milking the same cow in the same old way for all our revenue. I am proud of the Acting Minister of Finance on broadening out and adopting a policy that will not bring the forces of this House into great antagonism.
Let me say for the good of the manufacturers of this country that they possibly could alleviate their own condition if they see anything facing them that scares them. First, I would recommend that our manufacturers go down to their offices and unlock their doors at seven o'clock, instead of living in better houses than other classes who are watching them closely, living expensively, dressing gorgeously, driving expensive cars, taking long holidays and neglecting their business. If you say to them: "Why can you not get hold of your business as your fathers did?" they will say: "Oh, I have an organization; I cannot dissolve that organization; if business should pick up and the organization was dissolved, I could not handle the business because the organization would be gone." I put the question personally to some of those men. I have an illustration of a man who left Scotland more than fifty years ago. He came to a growing city in Canada and he went into the clothing business. He was his own buyer, his seller, his cutter and his accountant. If he had any assistants, he was the man that guided them on. He built up from a small business to a larger business, a larger business. No less than eight different places did he enlarge. Before his death-and he died too soon-he built a large manufacturing establishment in which he put the name of the company, and he hoped that it would continue. When the son came into the business and one other person whom I well know, I happened to go into the place, and what did I notice? I observed as I went in at the door, that the office had been fitted up with $5,000 worth of mahogany. It was gorgeous, I assure you. Not very many years after I happened to visit the place, and the man whose father had built up the business said:	"Things are going bad; do
you know where I can get $100,000?" I said: "When I came upstairs, I cast an eye back at the office and I noticed that what you call your organization were not busy; I observed that the female members were chewing gum and probably pinching themselves in order to keep from going to sleep. I noticed that the men were not working. I know another organization that has three stenographers, a financier and an-

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin

other man to assist. The man sat in his office and he wrote five-page letters when two sentences would have been better, and his business went to the dogs. " Now," I said, "young man, will you take an old man's advice?" He said: "This is getting desperate, and I do not know where I am going to land." I said:	"Would you rather face
bankruptcy than go down to the office with a smile and say to them: 'My father built up a business that I have inherited. He knew his business but I do not know mine. I must come into the office to-morrow morning at fifteen minutes before seven, unlock the door, learn the business and see where I am going.' " His organization was costing hinj twenty dollars where it should not have cost him over two dollars, and I am right. I might expatiate further, but that is a criterion of what is going on throughout this country. The young men should take their father's place and go down to the business and learn it. When a customer comes in and asks him a question, they will say: "Oh, I do not know, I will find Tom, Dick or Harry." That is true, not in one business alone, but in thousands of businesses that have an organization that is running the business. Be it to the credit of the Jew, he has the clothing business of the United States largely and he will have it in Canada because he is running the organization. Some day he will have saved up enough in salaries to buy the institution which others cannot handle.
I heard the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) speak about free trade in 1920, I think-and he made a fine speech-but in his concluding remarks he said that while it is good in theory, it cannot be in practice, because practically every country in the world is to-day under a protective tariff and therefore we have to have one. I have heard the first leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Crerar) say that we have to have revenue and we have to have a tariff to raise it. During the present session I heard the leader of the Progressive party (Mr. Forke) say: "I would not support a measure that would cripple one legitimate industry in Canada."
I ask you, Mr. Speaker: Has the Acting Minister of Finance kept faith and brought down a budget as well as any other man in this House could do? The question was a great one to cope with. In my opinion, although I have not spoken to him nor sent a delegation or any advice,-and I think that is something remarkable throughout this House he has looked at every thing in the country from all angles. If we consider the 
remark that has been made by the leader of the Progressive party that he would not cripple or do injury to one legitimate industry in Canada, is it right for our Acting Minister of Finance to bring down in this House a measure that will assist those who for two sessions have been hammering away in this House? I am not criticising them for doing that; they knew best their personal trouble, but there was about their speeches a personality that was astonishing to the old liners.
The people in the province of Quebec have had their troubles just as the people in the West and in the Maritime provinces have had. Indeed, it has been pretty much the same all over the country so far as the agriculturists are concerned. But we have had to take our medicine. W; have heard from the official opposition during the past two years, and particularly from the leader of that party (Mr. Meighen) the statement oft repeated that we on this side are more protectionist than the Conservative party. And shortly before the budget was brought down the right hon. gentleman said that we had only to wait and see and we should find that when the budget was disclosed nothing would be done. I d'o not think that anybody outside the cabinet had the slightest inkling as to what the budget would reveal, but personally I had perfect confidence in the course the Acting Minister of Finance adopted when he delivered what I think was the shortest budget speech that has been made in this parliament in many years. I believe that the minister has acted boldly and courageously in the interests of the greatest number of the people.
I submit that we ought to stand at his back and support him, and if his proposals do not succeed as well as we hope, then they can be changed. As a protectionist I would not only do what the minister has done; I would go further; I would adopt the tariff of the United States in many respects. They are exporting to this country over $90,000,000 of agricultural products, and I suppose that it is because the agriculturists in this House were sincere in their free trade professions that they did not insist on being protected themselves. But I think that we might have kept the agricultural products of the United States out of this country just as they do ours, because I believe in self-preservation. However, there are more years ahead of us, and in the meantime I support the present budget believing that no harm will be done the great industries in my country. There has been a great deal of hue and cry on the part of the woollen manufacturers; but I think that the

The Budget-Mr. Baldwin
reduction in the sales tax will about equal the preference on English goods coming here. I hope so at any rate, and I trust that things will work out well for the woollen men. On the whole I think the minister has given us a balanced budget; there is a surplus of some 830,000,000 in the year's operations and there will be saved to the taxpayers for the next year $24,000,000, How could the Acting Minister of Finanee have done better in the face of present conditions.
MacLean's magazine has been writing a lot about the scandalous extravagance of the government and has been comparing the Liberal party to the Conservative party with its corruption; it has been talking about graft in connection with everything, and has dealt particularly with the over-manned Civil Service. I do not wonder that there has been an uprising in this country when we have had the Civil Service increased by the late government from 11,000 to 60,000. It is not surprising that some able man in the press gallery should have undertaken to write the thing up. I have copies of MacLean's magazine and I presume every other hon. member has; and in the face of these facts, what do hon. gentlemen expect, in the name of common sense, that the Acting Minister of Finance should have done but to have brought down such a budget as we are considering to-night? Was he to have given us the old see-saw budget without making any effort to alleviate the conditions of the poorer people? I am pleased indeed that the government should have reduced the Civil Service by some 8,000. Suppose we had a business man who acted in a pussy-footing sort of way, wintering in California or Florida, what would one expect from such a man? Yet this is the type of man who would pray in this fashion;
O! Almighty Dollar! Thy shining face
Bespeaks thy wondrous power.
Make my pocket thine abiding place.
I need thee every hour.
Let the manufacturers sympathize with the labourer and the farmer. I happen to be one of those who rise at five-thirty every morning and even earlier, and I work fifteen hours a day. I do not like being personal to this extent, but I think that a little outspokenness occasionally does no harm. I have lived nearly seventy years and there is not a betterfeeling man in all Canada. I live for the joy of living and work cheerfully, and in the long run I think the cheerful worker has everyone beaten to a showdown. I have demonstrated that hard work hurts neither man, woman nor child. Indeed, some people contend against child labour, but I would let children work if
they wanted to. If we did we would have better men and women.
Now, my hon. friends opposite are shouting protection all the time, and this cry was their only hope in the election campaign of 1921. But it did not avail them anything.
I might say that the man who opposed me in my county lost his deposit, and I had a thousand to spare on my side.
Mr. SUTHERLAND; The hon. member was not talking free trade then.

No, sir, and neither am
I now advocating such a policy, but let me tell you something that was said at the nomination convention. A most distinguished lawyer from Montreal got up and said:	"If
you vote for W. K. Baldwin the people in Magog who work for the Dominion Textile Company will go with empty dinner pails, if they do not even eat rats." But I feared no such talk as that; I am like my hon. friend from Brantford (Mr. Raymond)-there is a closer relation between myself and my constituents than dollars and cents. My constituents live honourably and work hard, and they are charitable to the poor and the deserving. There is not one of them who is an autocrat.
Talking about the customs tariff. I have an absolute experience to relate. I received from Lamonte, Illinois, some very alluring prices on aluminum ware. For instance, teakettles for which I would pay $3.50 in Ottawa in war time were quoted at 80 cents, and every article on the long list was subject to a special discount of 25 per cent during the month of February. After several lists had been sent to me I called up the customs office at Coaticook and asked the tariff on aluminum-ware. They informed me the rate was 30 per cent. Thereupon I sent my order, and in due course the goods came forward. I sent the triplicate invoices down to the customs offices. Did I pay 30 per cent, Mr. Speaker? Not at all. It was plus, plus, plus. The duty came to slightly over 40 per cent. Well, the sale that I had on was slightly embarrassing to me, because on an order of $124.85 the duty amounted to $48.75. The freight was remarkably low, for in that great centre of Chicago they get exceptionally low rates to New England points, and it seemed to me that they got a very low rate indeed to the town of Coaticook. I have no fault to find with the great school of experience, which is the best educator in the world, but I assure this House that the next aluminum ware I want I will order from Oakville, Ontario,-just a little south of the constituencies represented by the Toronto members. Certainly I shall not send
The Budget-Mr. Baldwin

any more orders to the United States, for the duty is not what it appears to be. I am told that when the rate of duty is 40 or 42 per cent the actual percentage paid by the importer is over 50 per cent. So what in the name of common sense is the Manufacturers' Association hollering about? If that is not protection enough for them, what do they want?
I had not intended speaking on the budget, but I have been prompted to address the House by reason of some criticism that I heard in Montreal the other day from the Manufacturers' Association respecting the budget, They have worked very, very hard to get me into the Association, but I prefer to run my own business rather than allow any organization of manufacturers to run it for me. I want to be in touch with my business and be able to do the dirtiest job; while other people are dreading such things. I never saw a dirty job yet that could not be fixed all right with soap and water. If any men are losing business as a result of the budget, I ask them to live as modestly as do the members composing the Progressive group; I ask them to economize, to tell their dear wives, "I am not making so much money, perhaps, as you think I am, and probably it is our neighbours after all who tell you how rich I am." It is a very common practice for an acquaintance to say, "If I had your money I would do so and so." But so far as I am concerned, I spend my money to the extent of my credit, and I do so for the development of this great, grand and glorious Canada, as I am a Canadian first, last and all the time. I believe that we should go north and develop our great resources. I see the hon. member for East York (Mr. Harris) is in his seat. The other night-and I say it in all kindness -he was telling about the Laurier government building a railroad away in the northern part of Quebec. He knows what I am going' to say now. I say to him, "Just cast your eye on the map and you will see that more than nineteen-twentieths of the great province of Quebec is north of the railway."
Will the hon. member tell us about the population north of the railway?

There are few people there; but I believe there is untold wealth in that country awaiting development, and I am willing to risk the money I have to help find it. It is claimed that the gold vein which is making the province of Ontario so rich runs through northern Quebec down to the Labrador coast and up to Hudson straits. I

ask hon. members to visualize the wealth that God in His wisdom has placed in the midst of that country-wealth that will enrich the Dominion. The great clay belt alone is capable of producing immense wealth. When I read in the newspapers the troubles and deaths by accidents at the coal mines in the United States I say to myself: Canada should rid herself of paying the United States $100,000,000 a year. Instead of sending all this money out of the country we should create a better, a cleaner and a more serviceable power in our own country than we can generate from American coal. Eventually our water-powers will warm us as well as give us power and light.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I stand at the back of the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr Robb) because he has had the boldness and the courage to bring down a budget that few men in this House would have dared attempt. I congratulate him on his sound discriminating judgment.

Mr. Speaker, it is my intention to speak very briefly on several aspects of the budget. The effect of the budget and of the subsequent addresses delivered by several hon. members on the other side of the House, particularly by the members of the government, has been to create a feeling of uncertainty and apprehension throughout industrial Canada. A further result has been to bring the issue of protection more prominently before the House and before the country.
Last year there was an increase in the British preference on knitted goods, and in spite of the bad effect that that had upon industry, this year there has been another reduction in the tariff on farm implements. The injury brought about by these changes in the tariff has been greatly increased by the suggestion involved in the hope expressed by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) that these reductions should be the death knell of protection. Last year I pointed out to the House the serious consequences which the increase in the British preference would have upon the woollen industry of this country. There has been sufficient evidence before us during the past year, both through statements in the press and in speeches made in this House, to justify fully the warnings which were given at that time. I think it was the hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion) who made the statement in the House not long ago that 40 per cent of the machinery in our woollen mills had been closed down.

The Budget-Mr. Senn
Now, these are the results which we have already seen in respect to the change in the tariff on woollen and knitted goods, but there are results which we have not yet known anything about. Our woollen industries and our knitting industries are struggling along as best they can to retrieve their position and to keep their heads above water. There is a certain amount of momentum which a well regulated and a well organized industry always has which enables it to carry along for a certain length of time even under adverse circumstances, but if those conditions do not improve that momentum must gradually fail.
I could inform the House, if I were at liberty, of companies who are in the woollen business who did not feel the immediate effect of the increase in the British preference, whose sales for the past three months of this year have been practically cut in two compared with their sales of a year ago. Many companies are in the same predicament, and the result must be that large numbers of their factory operators will be thrown out of employment and possibly will have to migrate to the States to earn a living for themselves and their families.
There is every indication that the volume of imports will go on increasing. I have in my hand a clipping from the Daily News Record, a financial paper published in New York, of the issue of April 21st, 1924, which shows very clearly that the people across the line are looking to Canada for an outlet for their surplus product in woollen and knitted goods. The caption of the article should, I believe, demand the attention of hon. members. It is this:
Canada One of Largest Outlets for all Classes of Knit Goods.
The article says:	[DOT]
Canada forms one of the largest foreign outlets for nearly all classes of knitted goods, especially cotton and silk hosiery, and cotton underwear, the greatest bulk of imports of these articles being from the United States. Great Britain, however, practically controls the market in Canada for foreign made knit goods.
It goes on to state the amount of cotton, woollen and silk hosiery imported during the past year, showing that the total value of the import of these articles was 85,100,000 for the fiscal year ending March 31st, 1923, as compared with $2,800,000 in 1922. It points out also that for the fiscal year 1923 the share of Great Britain in the 9 p.m. total import was 63 per cent. It says further that although the United States share of this trade has shown a marked increase, Great Britain still retains
a strong hold on the market for wool hosiery-and underwear. That is sufficient to show the House, I believe, that the United States as well as Great Britain are looking to Canada for an outlet for their woollen and knitted goods. Another significant fact is that Mr. Walter Schwaebsh has been in Canada recently on a mission to promote the sale of German knitted goods. Among other things he told us while here, through an interview to the press, that the scale of German wages for woollen operatives was 40 cents per day. It is readily to be seen, how impossible it will be for our woollen and knitted goods manufacturers to compete with a wage scale of that kind.
I want to make a comparison between the duties imposed by the United States and by Canada on woollen goods and knitted goods, a comparison which I think will be of interest to the House. I have taken for the purposes of comparison the line of knitted sweaters, which are sold at the rate of 815 per dozen by the British manufacturer. The Canadian duty under the British preference on these articles is 20 per cent, which amounts to 83 a dozen, while the American duty on the same line of goods is 45 cents per pound, and 50 per cent ad valorem, which amounts to $9.75 per dozen. This is only a sample of what might be shown in artificial silk goods, stockings, and so on. I have made this comparison to show the difference between the attitude of the United States toward their industries and their workingmen and that which has been adopted by the government of the day in this country. The result is that our operatives are leaving Canada every day to go to help build up the protected industries of other countries particularly the United States.
Under the tariff regulations of 1923 a duty was placed on artificial silk fibre coming into Canada. We were informed by the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) that its purpose was to encourage the establishment of an artificial silk industry in Canada. Incidentally I might say that that was an acknowledgement by him of the value of protection. A duty was also placed on artificial silk tops, which are very largely used in our spinning mills. I am credibly informed, however, that this new industry which was expected to be in operation at the beginning of next year does not intend to manufacture artificial silk tops, therefore there is no necessity for adding duty to them with a view to encouraging their manufacture here. This matter has been

The Budget-Mr. Senn
drawn to the attention of the Finance Minister on more than one occasion, but as yet no remedy has been applied. It seems too bad that our Canadian manufacturer has to buy these silk tops at a higher rate because of this duty than does the British manufacturer who is selling his goods in competition with ours in the case of the finished article. In'spite of the very apparent result of the increase in the British preference upon the woollen and knitting industry the government have seen fit to reduce the duty- on agricultural implements. It is contended that this has been done for the purpose of aiding agriculture,, but I feel sure that instead of aiding agriculture it will in the end have a disastrous effect.
There is no use denying the fact that agriculture in Canada to-day is not in a prosperous condition. There may be some difference of opinion as to the reason for this, but I believe there are three reasons, briefly stated: The first is the loss of purchasing power in Europe. The second is the high tariff walls raised by the United States against our products, and the third is the large importation into Canada of agricultural products from the country to the south. The third reason, it seems to me, is the most important one and the one to which you must turn for a remedy for the existing state of affairs to-day.
It goes without saying that we have little or no control over the purchasing power of Europe, nor over the tariff barriers imposed by the United1 States, but it should be the duty of the Canadian government to do everything possible to adjust conditions in respect of the unequal deflation of prices. As usual the government has proceeded in the wrong way. The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) said in his speech last Monday as reported on page 1338 of Hansard:
We took into consideration the fact that we should, not to any extent, injure the manufacturers of farm implements in Canada, and it is not the desire of the government to interfere with the interests of any industry in Canada. But let me say that, when the full effects of these reductions are felt and when the encouragement which will be given to agriculture permeates through the business of Canada, there will be less unemployment and less emigration to the United States than under existing conditions to-day.

If the farmer could get the full benefit of the reduction in tariff on the price of these implements it would only mean a very small amount per year, taking the average life of these implements at ten years-in any case it would not amount to over $10 a year.
