Could anything be more absurd than to have a minister of the Crown stand in his place in this House and intimate that because a farmer is going to enjoy a $10 reduction of yearly cost in his implements the government has removed all his difficulties and that all he has to do is to go ahead and prosper. The government are really saying to the farmer "We cannot do anything to increase your revenue, but if you are not prospering we will see to it that other industries are not prospering either-we will do our best to destroy the market you have in our own centres of population."
Before agriculture can prosper in Canada the price of farm products must be equalized in comparison with that of other commodities. In my opinion the way to do this is not to seek to reduce the price of other commodities by the lowering of the tariff wall, thus driving our industries out of business, but to strive to bring the price of farm produce to a higher level. Our people were never so prosperous as when prices were on the high level, of years such as 1920-21. The way to accomplish this is to retain and to enlarge our home market. In spite of a determined effort on the part of certain hpn members to minimize the value of our home market, it is and will continue to be our greatest asset.

' The Budget-Mr. Senn
The Minister of Agriculture the other night, when .speaking on his estimates, expressed the view that the imposition of high duties would increase the price of farm products. He was discussing apples at the time but the inference was plain. I contend very strongly that instead of trying to lower the price of commodities which farmers have to buy-by reducing the protective tariff-and incidentally increasing imports and driving our people out of the country to find employment-we should keep them employed and keep them consuming our own farm products. These they would be able to purchase even under a higher tariff which would increase prices.
The hon. member for Queens (Mr. Sinclair) spoke in the same strain as the Minister of Agriculture. He went to considerable length in trying to convince the House that it was not necessary to increase the duties on farm products. Among other things he made special mention of fresh fruit and cheese, and tried to convince the House that the importations of farm products were largely of a kind not produced in Canada. He also told us that a large percentage of the fruits imported were not of a kind produced in Canada, and that the same was true about the importations of cheese. I do not wish to contradict these statements but let me say that every bit of imported fruit and every pound of imported cheese consumed in Canada displaces just that much of our Canadian products.
Then again in regard to eggs. The minister told us that the great bulk of imports are made during the months of December, January and February, just at the time when our own production is at its lowest. The same is true of vegetables. But the effect of the low duty on these articles is that the American producer has been and is still enjoying the benefit of the Canadian market when it is at its best-in other words, he gets the cream while the Canadian producer gets the skimmed milk. There is another side to this question as well. Importations of farm produce at that time of high prices displaces our eggs and vegetables, which are being held and have not been disposed of. I think the Minister of Agriculture the other night made the statement that our cold storage eggs were second to none in the world. I cannot see what difference it makes to the Canadian consumer whether he gets his first taste of new potatoes or fresh eggs in April or later on so long as he gets it at some season of the year. The ordinary artisan or labouring man does not buy new potatoes when prices are at their peak. It is only the well-to-do that benefit from the importation of American
products when our prices are high. The producer and the artisan get the worst of the deal both ways. One way we can help agriculture is by increasing and enlarging the home market. There is another way, I think, in which we can benefit very largely as agriculturists. We need a substantial reduction in freight rates. The Ontario farmer is suffering very materially from high freight rates, and I believe great injustice was done him by the restoration of the Crowsnest pass rates in 1922. Mr. Beatty, president of the Canadian Pacific Railway, made the statement before the Transportation Costs Commission that the chief objection to those rates was the fact that it would prevent the downward revision of rates in Canada generally. These rates affect my own constituency very seriously. I do not think there is a constituency in the province of Ontario which ships more hay and straw than my own. These commodities are naturally very bulky and the freights are very heavy. Most of these commodities are shipped only a short distance, namely 60 miles to Toronto, and yet the freight rate on hay and straw leaving the five principal shipping points in my own constituency amounts to $2.75 a ton. . There are many thousand tons shipped out during the year, and if we could only have the same reduction of freight rates which the farmers of the West were granted by the restoration of the' Crowsnest agreement it would amount to thousands of dollars to the farmers in that neighbourhood.
It is difficult to understand in the face of the serious situation forced upon the woollen and knitting industries by last year's tariff reduction, why the government will threaten the existence of other industries by tampering with the meagre protection which is now afforded. One is forced to the conclusion that the retention of office is the government's first consideration and that it is of more importance than the welfare of our industries.
I am not in a position to speak about the West but am free to say that the Ontario members of the Progressive group do not represent agricultural Ontario on this question. The Ontario farmers spoke in no uncertain way in the reciprocity election of 1911 and will do so again at the very first opportunity. They realize the value of the home market and the policy which will appeal to them more than any other is one which will retain and enlarge their home market; a policy of adequate protection not only for the manufacturing industries but for their own agricultural product.

The Budget-Mr. Pritchard

In rising to speak for a few minutes on the budget, I feel that it is fitting to make some reference to the fact that death has again visited our midst. While it has not taken one of our number from us, it has affected a gentleman who has occupied one of the first positions in our land, and to-day we have a number of the members of the government prominent in the public life of the country who have not been able to appear in their places on account of ill health. We are again brought to think of the lines:
Lives of great men all remind us
We can make our lives sublime,
And, departing, leave behind us
Footprints in the sands of time.
We are sorry to think that men who -have occupied prominent positions in this land for a number of years will, we fear, never again enter into the active duties of this parliament. I do not want to be pessimistic, but I think we all believe that; and furthermore some of us who believe we are in the activities of life, when we stop to think, realize that it will only be a few short years until we also will be called upon to depart from the scene of our present activities. May it be said of us as we can honestly say of some of our predecessors that we also have played our part in the work allotted to us.
Perhaps I might also pay the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) the compliment of saying that while his budget does not please us altogether-for some of us are very hard to please I will confess-it is perhaps a step in the right direction. Now I am going to give my opponents credit for being sincere in their endeavours to do something in the interests of Canada, so far as our trade relations are concerned. I would like for a short time to view the situation as it exists, and to see what the actual conditions are today. Any remarks I may make are based on what I have heard while sitting in this House for two years; and, in common with the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. McBride)-and I came from the same stock politically as the hon. member-I have been persuaded more and more as I have listened to the debates in this House, of the weakness of the arguments of those who are endeavouring to build up this country by a high tariff wall. Perhaps there are no arguments from any comer of the House that have convinced me of the fallacy of their contention more than those which they themselves, have advanced. I have listened to their speeches with great interest, and I will endeavour to-night to make a few remarks about some of them, to

show what I consider the illogical line of argument they are endeavouring to pursue.
What is the condition in this country today? We hear from that corner of the House to the left of you, Mr. Speaker, of the terrible disaster that has overtaken the manufacturers of this country-the same disaster that has been overtaking them for the last two or three years-and they connect it with the budget which we are discussing to-day. The protective policy has been in operation for about forty years and if there have been any results affecting the economic condition of the country these results have been brought about by the tariff which these hon. gentlemen and their predecessors put into force. We have proceeded, by an over-industrialized condition to bring about a situation in this country, as I remarked the other night, where we have more manufacturing concerns than can find a market for their products. These hon. gentlemen admit that Canadian manufacturers are unable to sell commodities to any other country; but now they wish us to bring other manufacturers into the country and support them, if possible, in order that they may in this way build up the country. I can think of the proposition in no other way than as that of a man endeavouring to lift himself up by the lugs of his boots. It is just as impracticable.
The hon. member for Fort William and Rainy River (Mr. Manion), speaking before six o'clock, endeavoured to show us that while we were paying the taxes, the manufacturers were really paying them. I would like to see how he reasons it out. The manufacturers fix their price, and when they are fixing their price they add their labour, all their taxes, municipal and every other kind, all the cost of the products, all the overhead expenses, and charge everything up to the consumer. We all share in paying the tax to the manufacturer, and as I think the hon. member for East Toronto (Mr. Ryck-man) said, we pay even the sales and income taxes. But another hon. gentleman says we do not pay them. Whom are we to believe? Let us look into the situation.
These gentlemen say they cannot carry on unless they have adequate protection. I would like to know how much would be adequate protection. While in Toronto at Easter I was talking to a gentleman and he said "If I were fixing the tariff I would make it so high that the sun would not shine over it." I said, "In any event, suppose you should make the tariff as high as Haman's gallows, what then?" He will stop all intercourse with outside and he will succeed in

The Budget-Mr. Pritchard
developing this country into a manufacturing country. After he has done that, what is the manufacturer going to do with his product? He tells us to-day that he cannot compete with England because they have cheap labour, and he cannot compete with the United States because they have dear labour. What does he want? He will tell us on the one hand that people coming to this country from Europe are going to the United States to produce stuff that they are selling, in many cases, 20 per cent cheaper than the home market with dear labour.
I want to go back to the question of the fruit situation which I was discussing the other night, as I did not bring out my argument fully with regard to that. The hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), when speaking on the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne, was looking over the statistical reports, and he showed the quantity of agricultural products that we, instead of growing ourselves, were importing from the United States. I think when some of the hon. gentlemen here began to look into and analyse his figures, they found that quite a quantity of that stuff was in the nature of oranges and other fruit that we cannot grow successfully in this country. I believe they do grow them in Ottawa; if not, they grow them in Guelph in very limited quantity as an experiment in hothouses, Supposing we take the hon. member's suggestion and produce this stuff in our country. We start at Ottawa, put up a large hothouse plant and employ a number of men to grow oranges and bananas and all that kind of fruit. We develop a wonderful industry at Ottawa. We then say: "Oh, we cannot make it pay; we must get protection; we shall have to raise the , duty on oranges and bananas coming into Canada because we are not making any money in this business and we cannot afford to let these people go out of employment. Look what it will mean. These people will go to the United States because we are not giving them work growing oranges and bananas in Ottawa." Hon. members may think this is ridiculous, but it seems that nothing short of extremes will show these hon. gentlemen the fallacy of their argument.
I remember Mr. Speaker while addressing some of us whom he was entertaining at luncheon, saying that the members of this parliament should be like a board of directors. I should like to look at this matter from that angle for a few minutes, because I thought the suggestion a very good one. We have been advised from the corner where we get so much advice, that we should go into mixed farming. Let us look at that suggestion for
a little while. We have a great big farm here in North America, about 4,000 miles one way and about 1,000 miles, more or less, the other way. It is a wonderful farm. We have the finest wheat fields in the world; we have the finest timber reserves in the world, and back in that stony ridge we have the finest mines in the world. We have the greatest fisheries in the world, and the greatest country in the world to absorb a population that is willing to get down to business and produce. But what is the reason that, with this tariff policy for forty years in this country of ours, we have a population of scarcely 9,000,000 people, and we cannot keep them here to-day when they do come. What is wrong? Is it free trade that has brought about that condition? Do you tell me that Canada is prosperous when we stood up in this House last session and opposed the immigration policy of the government of bringing in people from Europe whom we could not keep, and in order to bring them here taxing the people on the land who could hardly make a living? We know we have a country that can support
100.000.	000 people; yet we cannot support
9.000.	000 people, and we are talking about unemployment. What is the reason for unemployment? We have this big farm, and the policy of the government was to put people on that farm. But what did you do with the few Scotchmen who came over here and who came to Ottawa after this session began? Did you give them any employment? You could not give them employment in your manufacturing establishments, although you have been developing them for forty years and you say that you are building up this country. The farmers could not pay the wages. Why? Organized industry and organized labour have fixed their prices, and they dictate to the consumers what they shall pay for the product of their labour and their plant; whereas the other half, or a little more than half of the population, having no organization to control the price of their output or the price of their labour, have to compete with the cheap labour in Europe, and they are doing that.
Hon. gentlemen talk about keeping the Canadian dollar at par. Look at the statistical reports and see where the money is coming from. Is it coming from the manufacturers or from the farmers of Canada who are working for a dollar a day? If those men cannot make their businesses pay, why do they not follow the example of the farmers, either do the Work themselves or go out of business? They will not do that. Last session we had a howl from the woollen

manufacturers. They came to Ottawa repeatedly because there was a little reduction in the tariff on goods coming from Great Britain. Not long ago I picked up the papers and noticed where one of those woollen manufacturers, in this ruinous year of their business, was declaring a dividend of 7 per cent. There is an island in Muskoka-I think they call it Penman's island-of about fifty acres where you will find launches, boats, and I do not know what all. There is another gentleman who comes from a constituency somewhere around Hamilton who also has an interest in that island. What do you find? I believe the manufacturers of the wealth of this country are the producers in whatever sphere they may be moving. If they are not producers, they do not deserve to have the luxuries and the good things of this life. If they toil not, they should not have anything for a reward. When I was making a comparison between the daughters back on that island in the summer time and some of the daughters on the farm, I could not help thinking that back on that island at Muskoka: "They toil not, neither do they spin: And yet I say unto you, that even Solomon in all his glory was not arrayed like one of these."
Where did the money come from? I suppose it came from their fathers in Toronto. They do not want to pay the income tax, they have been telling us from that comer of the House that they should not pay the income tax; that we are interfering with industry. They claim that it is perfectly legitimate for 90 per cent of the money of this country to go into the possession of one-tenth of the people, to be exploited and done with just as they please at the expense of the 90 per cent. I feel that we want a policy that will give at least 50 per cent of the money to 90 per cent of the people. But they personally refuse to stand for anything of the kind. They say that they will fight anything that will interfere with the conditions under which they are living. They have been endeavouring constantly ever since this House met and since I came to this parliament to show that farming is paying.
I have been a practical farmer and there are a good many practical farmers in this comer of the House. I have been told-and I know this is correct-that for quite a number of years there were in this parliament few practical farmers, and I think the business of the country is showing the result of that to-day. We have had men trying to represent us in parliament who do not 
know agricultural conditions. These hon. gentlemen could get away with all this kind of stuff and make people believe it. When we consider the fight that we have to put up in this House to convince the intelligent representatives of this country of the actual facts, it is astonishing to me to think that we should be obliged to reiterate the facts year after year before we can get them to be admitted. Is it possible that men are ignorant of them, or is it that they do not wish to accept the actual facts when they are convinced of them? I do not know which alternative to take. I know that in some cases it is due to ignorance of the situation; but in other cases I am sure that those who refuse to admit the facts are doing so wilfully.
I referred a moment ago to the peculiar situation as regards the competition of our manufacturers, with the cheap labour of England on the one hand and the dear labour of the United States on the other. We farmers produce our goods and sell them to the men who are engaged at low wages in England. I have here an interesting little statement which I prepared in order to show the position of the working man in England as compared with that of the working man in Saskatoon, from the standpoint of the cost of living. And this is only one out of a number of items. The working man in England can buy 6i loaves of bread weighing 4 pounds to the loaf, which is a fairly good supply of bread for a small family for 7 days, and can have 15 cents a day over or SI .05 a week for milk. The working man in Saskatoon gets considerably less bread for the same amount of money; in other words, the man in London or Bristol gets 40 pounds of bread for $1.70 as against 25 pounds for $1.70 in Saskatoon. It is obvious therefore that the cost of living in Canada is too high. As a matter of fact I think this is the dearest. country in the world to live in. In the United States we can buy things 25 per cent cheaper, as was proved last year, in regard to a good many articles, in the inquiry which was held by the special committe on agriculture. And the same thing is true in England. Yet hon. gentlemen want to tax us stUl higher; they say that the tariff is not high enough. My opinion is that the tariff is not the whole trouble; I will admit that. Nevertheless the tariff is a considerable item in the high cost of living; and the wage trouble is one of the most difficult problems that we have to contend against. You cannot separate wages, taxes and the tariff; they are all interwoven. The question was asked the ex-Minister of

The Budget-Mr. Pritchard
Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) the other day, why the manufacturers could not sell in the United States; and he could not answer that question, because he was unable to. If the wages of the artisans were reduced to the level of the wages which the farmer is able to pay, the manufacturer would be able to sell his goods anywhere. But the working men refuse to adopt the standard of living which they expect the agriculturists to adopt. In order to exist on what the people in cities are willing to give them for their products, the farmers of Canada would have to live under the conditions of serfs; they would have to adopt the mode of life which some people say the Chinese and the Japanese follow. The; tariff is the issue, and it will be fought to the finish. It was said this afternoon by some hon. gentlemen that the tariff would be the issue before the country for some time to come, and I have no doubt as to the truth of that statement. We cannot, as I say, separate the tariff from the question of taxes and from the wages that are paid. In that direction I heard a criticism of the government by the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Anderson) the other night. The hon. gentleman was referring to what he termed the extravagance of the government in connection with the running expenses of the country, comparing the year 1914 with the years 1922, 1923, and 1924. I took the trouble to work out his figures from my way of looking at the facts and I found that wages had gone up practically 60 per cent in that time, whereas the expenses of the country had increased only 30 per cent. Allowing 50 per cent of the cost of running the country now for wages, it would appear that the country is being managed to-day at a lower cost than it was in 1914. A good many charges are levelled at our public institutions and our local legislatures on account of the extra cost which is involved at the present time in administration. But the great trouble to-day is the wage problem.
As a practical farmer I should like to state briefly what I would do, and what I think every intelligent farmer does. I would not attempt to grow oranges on my farm, nor would I raise peaches. As I said the other night, I looked around to see what my particular locality was adapted for growing, and when I ascertained that, I produced that crop. Hon. gentlemen talk about the home market, and it makes me tired. Every one of these high tariff men harp, upon that string, and it is no use laughing at them if we do not meet their arguments. They tell us that if we build up the cities we shall have a home market. Well, that would take 100
altogether too long; we should have to wait several hundred years for such a market, and we are too practical to do anything of the kind. We are told that we are producing too much wheat for the market, and the western farmers are described as miners and not farmers. When travelling through southern Alberta last summer, however, I met a real farmer, a man who was by no means a miner. Now, I believe there is some truth in that assertion; I will not altogether refute it. I believe we have men who are not good farmers. But this man had been on a farm twenty-five years and he had a good stable and a good pile of manure. He was taking care of it and I said to him, "Charlie, what are you doing with that pile of manure?" He said he could not do anything with it yet as his crop was ready to cut, The crop was very good in some places, while in other places it was quite heavy; and he said there was only one little spot where in twenty-five years he had found the slightest need of manure. Had he used the manure on his land it would have been all gone; but the time will come when it will be needed. In the older section of Ontario where we have been cropping the land for fifty years I can show any hon. gentleman farms that have been constantly cropped and are yielding as good crops to-day as ever in their history. And a hundred years hence they will be producing just the same. There is one difference between our farms, properly managed, and our mining and other industries. Our timber resources may-and will-fail, our fisheries may fail, our mines may be worked out; but you will never work the land out. The land will be a national asset for all time. And we have the promise that as long as the world stands seed time and harvest shall not fail.
Now, then, the question is:	Are we going
to encourage our basic industry, or are we not? They tell us that we have over-production of wheat. What did the most expert men to be found on the North American continent testify before the Agricultural committee two years ago? They stated, and I believe them to be correct, that every year a market is found for all the wheat the world produces. We know very well as practical farmers that in Ontario we can consume a great deal of the wheat that comes from the West. We are consuming screenings, and we want more of them. There is no duty on corn coming in from the corn belt of the United States, we have been getting it free of duty for the last forty years. We are not objecting to that. When it is shipped in from the United States to our market it does not seriously



The Budget-Mr. Pritchard
hurt our market because the surplus agricultural products of the United States will reach the same market as our surplus will go to eventually. The same remark applies to importations of eggs or butter or cattle. For instance, a drover from Toronto goes to Chicago and buys cattle by the trainload, brings them into this country and eventually ships them to Great Britain. What difference does it make to us? Ultimately they all go to the one market. As I said before, the 20 per cent exportable surplus regulates the price of the home market. And anything we cannot produce successfully and find a market for we have no business to produce at all. The other night the fruit situation was discussed, and we were told that our British Columbia fruit farmers cannot sell their product in this country without a protective tariff. I noticed in the paper a few days ago that British Columbia apples are shipped as far east as Nova Scotia. But I know for a fact that in the county of Oxford one of our fruit growers made a substantial profit on his apple crop. He did not care about protection; he could compete with the world in growing apples. Therefore when the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland) asks to have price regulation for farmers' produce I am astonished, for we have a soil and climate that will produce almost anything we need in the agricultural line, and consequently we have no competition to fear from any quarter of the globe.
Now, I do not wish to knock our industries, if they are essential; but I believe we have industries that we might as well be without. If they are not self-supporting and able to carry on business efficiently, I say they should be eliminated. We need manufacturing industries, but they should' follow agriculture in this country and not undertake to lead our national development. That is my opinion.
I believe that certain industries will have to be closed up, for we have too many. I remember fifty years ago in my town we had two foundries and! several other small industries. The people left the rural sections for the small towns, and eventually they left the small towns for the cities. What happened? The larger concerns came in and deliberately put the small industries out of business. Having killed the small industries and the small towns, the big fellows now are afraid they are going to be hit and they set up a howl. We had two of the finest packing plants in my district, but they were put out of business by the big packing interests, who used for the purpose the money they made out of our earnings, for they got it from nowhere else.

As I said before, the budget is not exactly what I would like to have seen. But. remember, I do not mean to say that I want greater reductions. What I want is to have the duties lowered on the necessaries of life for the working men. I am going to vote for the budget for the reason that I think the government have gone as far as I would ask them to go at the present time, but I believe the amende ment calls for something that in. the future we should have. But I am not going to lie down under the charge of being a free trader. I am not a free trader. I believe that the tariff should be lowered somewhat, for, as I said before, I think wages must be dealt with. The question of wages is the most difficult problem before us. That is one reason why I should like to have seen the resolution of the hon. member for Portage la Prairie (Mr. Leader) brought before the House and discussed intelligently. After hearing the complaints and charges brought by the Civil Service in this city against the government and against hon. members, I think we must admit that they have grounds for their contention that we are willing to cut the other fellow's income but not our own. In one sense I do not think we are getting too much. But Mr. Speaker are we here for dollars and cents or in the interests of Canada? If we are here for dollars and cents we are not worthy of our positions as representatives of the people. But I think we are here in the interests of the country, and that whatever is for the welfare of the Dominion as a whole we want to accomplish. I believe that we cannot convince these men of our sincerity until we set them an example. For my part, I am willing to deal with wages just as I would deal with the tariff, that is, I would apply a 12i per cent cut to every member of the government service who is getting $3,000 and over; I would not confine the cut to the Senate and the House of Commons. I would attempt to bring things back to a balance so that the man on the farm and the manufacturer could both hire their help and work together harmoniously. In this way we could develop agriculture and so create real business for the manufacturers. It will hit. some of our industries, but I believe it is quite possible, if agriculture gets a chance to develop, for it to soon create such a volume of business as will give all our manufacturers full opportunity. to employ not only their present hands but many additional ones.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think there is very much left to be said in connection with the budget; the ground has been pretty well covered. To

The Bridget-Mr. McBride
me the budget is a business statement and has been brought down in a businesslike way, and I think the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) and the government deserve a great deal of credit for bringing it down as they have.
A good deal has been said in connection with the tariff. A number of members on this side of the House criticised the people in British Columbia for trying to get a fair price for their apples. The other night they took up two hours of the time of the House on the subject. I hold in my hand a letter from the Grain-grower's co-operative organization which shows that organization makes 60 cents per box, whereas the man that raises and packs their apples only gets a dollar a box. I would ask some of my friends who is the greatest grafter jn that transaction, the man who raises the apples or the man who gets the 60 cents. Here is the letter, written by one of the officers of the grain-growers' organizations.
There are many points in connection with the tariff that might be touched on. I think that there was a tariff reduction coming to this country. I am not a free trader by any means, but I do think that the government deserve a great deal of credit for the reduction they have made and I hope to see them go still further in that direction later on.
A great deal has been said about the poor wage earner in this country. Some people make a special plea with regard to the wage earner; they seem to be always fighting the wage earner's battle. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Stevens) made the statement that about 50 per cent of the cost of manufacturing articles went in wages. I would like to quote a few figures in that connection. Before doing so, I wish to say that there has been a good deal of talk about the reduction of the tariff driving people from Canada to the other side of the line and also closing up our factories, but I see by reports from the other side that factories are closing up there also.	I saw an item in a
newspaper which stated that one United States factory had closed its doors and that 3,800 men had been thrown out of employment. If this cut in the tariff is throwing people out of work on the Canadian side I should think it would increase the activities of the factories on the other side, according to the statements of some members of this House, but people seem to be thrown out of employment in the United States just as they are here.
The following statistics were sent to me since the budget was brought down and since the statements about the poor workingman
100i
have been repeatedly made on the floor of this House. The figures are based 10 p.m. on what the workingman gets out of the manufacturers' cost, not the retail price. For instance, if the amount paid in wages based on the cost of manufacture was 18 cents, when it would get down to the consumer it would be about 9 cents. Now, here is what the wage earner gets on the dollar: in cotton goods, 17 cents; silks and woolens, 16 cenits; hosiery, 18 cents; glassware, 30 cents; sugar, salt and linseed, 3 cents; aluminum goods and gloves, 18 cents; shoes, that we hear so much about, 27 cents; carpet and rugs, 20 cents; gas engines, 23 cents; electric machinery, 23 cents. The writer of the letter I am quoting these figures from goes on to say:
A girl running a number of machines will knit 1,800 pairs of socks in a day, at a cost of 2 cents per dozen or one-sixth of one cent per pair.
Not very much in wages, is it? He goes on to say:
A man running a number of machines making spark plugs for automobiles turns out a spark plug in six seconds, at a wage cost of one-eighth of one cent.
That is what the poor workingman, whom we hear so much about, the man we are supposed to foe driving out of the country, gets out of making spark plugs. He says in conclusion:
The next time you hear any of your manufacturers wax eloquent on the high wages paid to factory workers in this country you can produce the above figures to them and ask them for an explanation.
I might say I have not got that explanation yet. Now I would like to say a few words on immigration. I saw in a Montreal paper a few days ago the following words uttered in a speech made by a certain gentleman-I do not know that I will take his name in vain just at this time. He said:	"The western
farmer and the city worker are both slaves." When I read that I could not help thinking that it was unfortunate for Canada that that class of people was allowed to land on our Canadian shores, as it is not in the best interests of Canada that such statements should be made. That- is not the kind of statement that will build up homes in this country or make our Canadians contented. We do want, immigration in Canada. I know out West it is a difficult proposition to get help on the farms. I am referring to British Columbia. We want immigration, but we do not want the class of immigration who is whining all the time. We want men who

Mr. McBride

are willing to work and to make Canada what it should be. After nearly thirty-two years of experience I am here to say that there is no country that offers such opportunities to a young man or young woman as Canada does. There are many resources here to be developed and the country offers many splendid opportunities.
There is another kind of immigration that we do not want. I will refer to that very briefly, because the hon. member for Comox Alberni (Mr. Neill) dealt fully with it the other evening. I am speaking now of oriental immigration and I want to thank this government for what they have done in the past in preventing the oriental from coming to our shores. This government have done more to put a stop to orientals coming to Canada than all other previous governments. They have practically stopped the Chinese from coming in; last year only about seven or eight entered Canada. I would ask them, however, to go a little further and to apply the same act to the Japanese. It has been said that the Japanese have very elevated ideas about their own ability and that the Canadian people do not want to hurt their feelings. What about their hurting the feelings of the Canadian people? What about their coming to a country where they know they are not wanted? No people know better than the Japanese and the orientals in general that they are not wanted in this country. In that case why should they have this right to come and impose themselves on the people of Canada? I would ask the present government to apply to the Japanese the same act that is now in force against the Chinese. If they do they will find themselves commended in history for keeping Canada a white man's country as Australia is doing.
There are one or two other questions I should like to bring to the attention of the House. It is true they are local in their character but they are not the less important because of that. One of them has to do with the transcontinental highway. When British Columbia entered confederation it was with the agreement that the Dominion government would build a railroad from east to west so as to connect the province with eastern Canada. At that time we had a highway from the coast up into the interior of British Columbia. Some people may say that that thoroughfare was not a first class highway, but I have talked with men who frequently used it in trading operations and when six yoke of oxen were able to haul ten tons of supplies the road could not have been a very bad one. In fact I will give some figures which the engineers of the Highways Commission have compiled to

further demonstrate its favourable character. They admit the liability of the government to put that road in repair. In the first place they say, "The old Cariboo road varies in places from twelve to eighteen feet wide." They also say that it was in fairly good shape when the Canadian Pacific railway was begun. According to the report of the Canada Highways Commission to the Department of Railways and Canals the location of the road, its grades, the crib work, retaining walls, and other engineering features were all of a high order. For many years after the construction the Cariboo road was the only trunk artery into the interior of the province, and tourist traffic along the scenic Fraser route has given a new value of importance to the old road. Traffic is now impossible, as about sixteen miles have been closed as a result of accumulation of slides caused by the construction of the government built railway. The report continues:
Owing to the utilization, in part, of the general location of the old Cariboo road, pursuant to the desire of the Dominion government as expressed in instructions to their engineers to secure a good serviceable, reliable railway with the least possible outlay, it would seem that the Dominion government, should not be called upon for the cost of rebuilding the Cariboo road, destroyed in construction of railways, unless the provincial government want to reconstruct the whole Cariboo road.
That is just what the provincial government is doing at the present time. It is constructing the road, and the people out there think the Dominion government should put into condition that portion of the road which was destroyed when the Canadian Northern and Canadian Pacific railways were constructed. The estimated cost of re-establishing that portion of the road injured by the construction of the Canadian Northern would be $153,897, and the making good of the damage done by the Canadian Pacific railway would amount to $217,500. Now the British Columbia portion of the latter railway was built by the Canadian government and accordingly the province's claim in connection with that line is a reasonable one. Under the federal Highway Act a splendid system to connect roads has been constructed on the coast side of the mountains, and also in the interior of British Columbia. The Fraser river road referred to being the only link connecting the two I should say it is exceedingly important that the Cariboo highway should be opened with the least possible delay.
As I have already explained it is in regard to these portions of the old Cariboo road which were destroyed by the railway construction referred to that I am requesting the assistance of this government. The Cariboo highway has been given the status of a

gazetted road by the provincial government, which to date has not abandoned any portion of that highway. I think it is up to the Dominion government to make a special grant in aid of the reconstruction of that road. According to the evidence of their own engineers it was the construction of Dominion railways that put the Cariboo highway out of operation and it is very important at the present time that that highway should be reconstructed. The estimated cost of the work,
I should explain, is about $1,500,000. The provincial government is not asking the federal authoritites to defray the whole cost of construction, but only a certain amount of the expense.	,
There is another matter I should like to bring up. It is in connection with the returned men and I regret that the Minister of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment is not in his place. At Tranquille in British Columbia there is a sanatorium, which accommodates quite a number of returned soldiers. Those men were deemed good enough to go overseas and fight for Canada. Unfortunately while they were there quite a number of them contracted lung disease and are now in this sanatorium. Some of them have been cured as far as the treatment at the sanatorium will allow, but when they leave the institution and return to the coast they find the climate there too damp for them and very often they experience a relapse. If they seek admission in boarding houses in Kamloops, or any part of that district they are not wanted. When they leave the Tranquille sanatorium they are looked upon by many people as actually having tuberculosis and consequently these poor fellows are not wanted in boarding houses, the other lodgers would not care for their company. If the government would make a grant of say $25,000 it would be possible to purchase ten or fifteen acres of land upon which ten or twelve cottages might be erected as an experiment. By making provision of this character the government would go a long way to satisfy the returned men at the sanatorium. When they left the hospital they could go there and enjoy some of the comforts of life, and have their wives and families with them. It seems to me to be pretty hard that men who went overseas and fought for their country should have to live divorced from their wives and families when they return to Canada. For that is what it means-the wife and family live at the coast while the man himself is compelled to reside in the interior because his health will not permit him to return to his loved ones. Now, a man at Kamloops with a cottage and an acre of land could raise all the vegetables he
needed and he would be kept employed for a large part of the summer. I think the government would be well advised if it would set apart an appropriation of $25,000 for the purpose of making this experiment.
There is still another matter to which I wish to allude. The Dominion government owns a telephone system in British Columbia. That province differs from the other provinces in the fact that it is very much cut up by mountains. You can go into some of the mountainous regions and find there only ten, fifteen, twenty or maybe fifty families who are practically isolated from the rest of the country. If the government would be a little more liberal in its appropriations for telephones better facilities could be provided for the people to whom I refer and they would be in a much more contented frame of mind.
While I am in favour of immigration being brought to this country, I have always maintained that a man raised on a farm in Canada is twice as valuable as the immigrant brought in. Men brought up in the country know its ways and can readily adapt themselves to varying conditions.
I should like to say just a word about the value of the telephone in helping to bring contentment to outlying and sparsely settled districts. There are districts where telephone lines have been installed and it seems to put new life into people and to make them content. I am not saying that it is the right and proper thing that the Dominion government should own the lines. I think it should be a provincial matter. However, I am taking the matter as it stands. The Dominion government owns these lines, and has owned them since confederation. I think it would be money well spent if the government would build a number of extensions in the outlying districts. The Minister of Public Works should give special attention to the question.
